items.title: Housing Market, Bathla, AI: Australia Briefing
body: Australia’s spring housing revival failed to materialize at the weekend, with the closely watched auction results in the capital cities remaining well below the same time last year.

Auction volumes were about 34% lower than this time last year, while clearance rates were at 58.5%  — a stark contrast to a year ago when almost three in four homes at auction were sold. The latest results are a further sign of weakening in the nation’s once-hot housing market following government property tax changes in May and three Reserve Bank interest-rate increases.

It’s leaving the Reserve Bank in a bind with a softening housing market almost certain to crimp spending through the wealth effect. The central bank is expected to hike its policy rate at least once more, possibly as early as this month, to quell consumer cost increases. But another lift to borrowing costs may further dent home prices, on top of forcing consumers to use any spare cash to service mortgages rather than discretionary spending.

That dynamic is sure to be a feature in Australian business and political news this week. The RBA’s economics chief, Sarah Hunter, is in Canberra speaking at a forum on regional Australia on Monday, before Governor Michele Bullock fronts parliamentarians on Friday. — Matthew Burgess, Melbourne Reporter

Staying with real estate, Bathla Group — the Australian developer that’s become the poster child for broader strains in the property and private credit markets — has just days to nail down something that’s proven elusive so far: longer-term financing needed to avoid liquidation. Far-right leader Pauline Hanson continues to stir controversy after a video she posted branding a fellow lawmaker and former soldier a “traitor” prompted a volley of insults and recriminations. The video from Hanson’s One Nation has consumed Australian politics in the past week after Liberal Party lawmaker Andrew Hastie, who served in the Middle East and is now shadow industry minister, denounced it for repeatedly leveling the insult at him.

The Autonomous Bougainville Government vowed to take action after alleged arson destroyed equipment at a giant Papua New Guinea copper mine that had recently begun efforts to restart almost 40 years after it was shut down. Heavy machinery and vehicles belonging to India’s Lloyds Metals & Energy — the Panguna mine’s newly appointed contractor — were destroyed in the fire, RNZ Pacific reported.

New Zealand’s opposition Labour Party pledged to raise the nation’s pool of retirement savings should it win the national election in November.  Contributions into retirement accounts by businesses would rise to 6% of a worker’s pay by 2032.

US equity futures fell and oil advanced as investors weighed renewed concerns over the pace of AI development against hotter-than-expected US inflation that bolstered bets the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates on Wednesday. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index declined 1.2% after the underlying benchmark gained 0.9% Friday. S&P 500 futures also fell in early Asian trading. Brent crude rose 2.8% to $107.55 a barrel.

A planned meeting for Monday between Iran and several Gulf nations on creating a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed, according to Oman’s foreign minister. Badr Albusaidi said in a post on X that the meeting is being delayed “in the interests of consensus,” without offering any details about next steps.

When Kevin Warsh was sworn into office at a White House ceremony in May, President Donald Trump praised his hand-picked Federal Reserve chairman and encouraged him to be “totally independent.” That latitude from the president will be tested this week as the Fed faces mounting pressure to hike interest rates to tame elevated inflation.

AI executives’ calls to slow development of the technology are likely to weigh on chipmaker and supply-chain stocks in the near term, but will probably have limited long-term impact as spending on computing infrastructure remains strong, market strategists say. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei said Saturday that the company would introduce additional safeguards and urged the broader industry to slow the pace of development of their most advanced models. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed the proposal, while xAI’s Elon Musk said “Dario is right.”
All times Sydney• 12:30 p.m.: RBA’s Hunter gives fireside chat

Tesla teased an Oct. 1 event to showcase its next-generation Roadster vehicle, a niche product that CEO Elon Musk first unveiled in November 2017.The event, which has been eagerly anticipated by Tesla fans, is likely to fuel even more speculation about a merger between Tesla and SpaceX. “Go for launch” is a nod to SpaceX’s rocket launches, and Tesla has used its live events to gin up enthusiasm among customers and investors.

items.title: Trump EPA to Rescind Carbon Standards for Coal, Gas Power Plants
body: The US Environmental Protection Agency is expected to formally rescind carbon pollution standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants as soon as Monday, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Trump administration’s latest major climate rollback is expected to come on the sidelines of a Group of 20 energy ministers’ meeting in Houston, said the people, who asked not to be named because the details aren’t yet public. Earlier this year, the EPA rescinded similar climate standards for vehicles and the 2009 endangerment finding, a landmark ruling which held that greenhouse gases threaten human health.

Under Trump, the EPA first proposed revising the power-plant climate rules last summer. This week, the agency is finalizing a piece of the initial proposal — scrapping Biden-era mandates requiring existing and future US fossil fuel-fired power plants to deploy specific emissions-reduction technologies, including carbon capture and storage, to sharply cut their greenhouse gas emissions in the coming decades, according to the people.

Agency officials also plan to propose a separate rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically pose a threat, effectively a separate endangerment finding for power plants under the Clean Air Act.

Power plants are the US’s largest industrial source of greenhouse gas emissions. If the US power sector were a country by itself, it would rank as the world’s sixth-largest emitter of greenhouse gases, according to a New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity analysis of 2022 emissions data.

Under former President Barack Obama, the EPA finalized the Clean Power Plan, which required existing and future fossil-fuel-fired plants to cut their climate pollution for the first time. The Supreme Court struck it down in 2022 and a separate court ruling struck down the first Trump administration’s replacement rule.

The EPA under former President Joe Biden finalized its own rules in 2024, which effectively forced the nation’s current fleet of coal plants to capture most of its carbon emissions by 2039 or close. This is the rule now being repealed.
The EPA didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Some utilities and power generators lobbied for the change, arguing the Biden-era standards were unrealistic and not economically achievable. The elimination of the requirements also dovetails with efforts by the Trump administration to keep coal-fired power plants in operation as more energy-hungry data centers and domestic manufacturing come online.
Environmental groups slammed the EPA’s retreat.
“This is a transparent giveaway to fossil fuel polluters, and the courts should see it that way,” said Maggie Coulter, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute.

items.title: Takaichi Ally Wins Okinawa Vote, Aiding Military Build-Up
body: A candidate backed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s ruling party ousted the incumbent governor of Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture in an election on Sunday, delivering a boost to the premier’s push for a stronger military to stave off threats from China.

Genta Koja won more than 50% of votes cast in the election, according to national broadcaster NHK, defeating Governor Denny Tamaki and giving Takaichi greater influence over the strategically important cluster of islands in the East China Sea that host the bulk of US military facilities in Japan.

“This election was a referendum on bringing about a fresh start and moving Okinawa forward,” said Koja, who at 42 becomes the youngest governor of Okinawa since it was handed back to Japan in 1972 by the US, which had been the occupying power after World War II.

While Tamaki, 66, has sought to move a major US military base out of Okinawa, Koja supports a plan for the base to remain in Okinawa in a new location. Koja’s victory may also make it easier for Takaichi to expand Japan’s own military footprint on its southern islands, which stretch toward Taiwan and have assumed greater strategic importance as Chinese military activity in the region intensifies.

“I accept the will of the people,” Tamaki said in conceding to Koja, who is part of a younger generation of Japanese more supportive of building up military power to counter challenges from China and North Korea.

Koja’s win adds to recent electoral gains for Takaichi in Okinawa after her ruling Liberal Democratic Party won all four of the prefecture’s seats in the Lower House election earlier this year for the first time.

The former deputy mayor of Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, campaigned on a platform of boosting wages and building a health and wellness industry in Okinawa to help drive growth. His campaign was backed by Takaichi’s LDP and other right-of-center political parties, with heavy hitters from the parties regularly appearing with him on the campaign trail.

“I would like to work closely with the new governor and do everything I can to strengthen Okinawa’s economy,” Takaichi said Monday in remarks to reporters. “As for other issues, we will respond appropriately while listening carefully to the views of the new governor,” she added.

Okinawa has traditionally been a center of resistance to US military bases, but the latest election result underscores a shift in the political debate away from that topic as China’s military activities increase near Taiwan and Japan.

“Looking at the global situation, there are problems that can’t easily be solved just by appealing for peace,” Koja said in an interview a few days before the election. “Our Self‑Defense Forces alone are not sufficient to maintain deterrence. I also understand that the Japan‑US. security framework is necessary,” he said.
Read: China Threat Erodes Japanese Anger Over US Bases Ahead of Vote

Koja’s election removes a source of tension with the central government over the planned relocation of the US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma base from densely populated Ginowan to the Henoko coastal area of northern Okinawa. Tamaki had tried to stop the relocation with legal action, but those lawsuits all failed and construction work has continued at the new site.

“I accept that relocating to Henoko is the fastest way to eliminate the dangers of the Futenma Air Station,” Koja said, noting residents’ concerns about the dangers of military aircraft flying close to residential areas.

Koja’s candidacy appeared to appeal to younger voters, who are more focused on economic concerns as incomes in Okinawa continue to lag the rest of Japan. An NHK exit poll found that over 70% of voters in their thirties voted for him.
Koja said that Takaichi’s plans for major investments in 17 strategic industries could help increase economic opportunities in Okinawa beyond its main income source from tourism.

“The Takaichi administration has plans to invest heavily in areas such as aquaculture with the aim of fostering the growth of companies. I hope we can make use of that in Okinawa,” he said in the interview.

items.title: Anthropic Expects an Operating Profit This Quarter, FT Says
body: Anthropic PBC told a small group of shareholders it will report an adjusted operating profit this quarter, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, marking a second consecutive period of profitability as the company prepares to go public.

The metric strips out certain exceptional or one-time costs. The artificial intelligence company’s gross margins exceed 80% before factoring in revenue-sharing payments to partners such as Amazon.com Inc. and training costs for AI models, people familiar with the matter told the paper.

The report comes as the Claude AI maker prepares for an initial public offering with the aim to match or exceed SpaceX’s record $86.3 billion offering earlier this year. The company chose the Nasdaq as its listing venue, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg News on Sunday.
Read More: Anthropic Expects to Match or Top SpaceX’s Record IPO Size

AI companies have rushed to lock in additional financing via share sales, debt sales and public listings as they contend with massive capital expenditure needs stemming from an insatiable demand for computing power. Anthropic was set to finalize a $15 billion revolving credit facility this month, Bloomberg News has reported.

While the industry has spurred a stock rally, growing concerns about potentially existential threats posed by rapidly improving AI technology have led key industry players to call for safeguards. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei was joined by OpenAI Inc. CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk on Saturday in calling for a slower pace of AI development, citing the escalating risks.
Read More:  Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development
Altman told Fortune in an interview that his company won’t go public this year, citing safety concerns.

Anthropic is on track to generate annualized revenue of more than $65 billion based on its current performance, up more than sevenfold from its pace at the end of last year, Bloomberg News previously reported.

items.title: Xi-Modi Thaw at BRICS Masks Deep Divisions Between Asian Rivals
body: Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first sit-down on Indian soil in seven years signaled a will to further repair ties and manage an unpredictable Donald Trump.
But fundamental differences remain despite the good vibes flowing from the 10-nation BRICS summit in New Delhi.

In a 45-minute meeting on Saturday, the two leaders agreed to take a strategic and long-term perspective on the relationship, further promote cultural and business exchanges, and coordinate on regional and global issues.
Sitting across from Modi, Xi recounted with a smile his first visit to India in 2014 to the state of Gujarat. “You received me in your home state on your birthday,” he said.
He went on to call China and India “partners rather than rivals, and development opportunities rather than threats to each other.” Modi, in turn, said “differences should not become disputes.”

The bilateral meeting was a symbolic moment for the world’s two most populous nations, which are emerging from a multi-decade low point in relations fueled by bloody border clashes and deep strategic distrust. The meeting allowed both countries to show the world that ties are on the mend at a time when each is navigating their own troubled relationship with the US under Trump.

However, beneath the show of unity, deep differences remain. The two remain far apart on their border dispute, with those differences on display in diverging readouts from each side following the leaders’ meeting: India said border peace was “essential” for ties to develop further, while Beijing issued its usual position of separating the boundary dispute from broader ties.
New Delhi also highlighted economic imbalances that have made India more reliant on China over the years, with a trade deficit that has doubled in the past decade.

“External factors, such as US policies and the ongoing wars, are driving the thaw, but I’d be cautious about calling it anything more than a thaw,” said Sana Hashmi, a postdoctoral fellow at Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation, a think tank. “There are still more divergences than convergences and China still sees India as a competitor.”

The New Delhi visit was capped by a joint BRICS statement that called for restraint in the US-led war in the Middle East and a rollback of tariffs and trade barriers. For Xi, whose country dominates the bloc politically and economically, the summit offered a platform to shore up his image as a global statesman capable of managing the newly fluid global order challenged by Trump. The BRICS summit comes just weeks before Xi’s expected visit to the US.

It’s “unmistakable optics — a clear show of unity and a signal to Trump as Xi prepares to visit Washington,” Julian Gewirtz, a former senior director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the White House National Security Council, wrote on X.

China-India relations entered a deep freeze in 2020, when a confrontation at their 3,488-kilometer (2,167-mile) frontier killed soldiers on both sides and drove relations to their lowest point in decades. Covid halted travel between the nuclear-armed neighbors, while India imposed restrictions on Chinese investment and technology.

Since then, the two sides have taken tentative steps to rebuild ties. Modi visited China in 2025, discussions have taken place on resolving border disputes, and direct flights between the two countries have resumed.

The body language between Xi and Modi at this weekend’s meeting showed a level of comfort between the two leaders, said Rajiv Dogra, an author and former Indian diplomat. It was the second time in a matter of weeks that they had been photographed holding hands as they spoke, following their recent meeting at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Kyrgyzstan.

“The visit, I would say, was consciously tailored to be on the hopeful side for the Indo-China relationship,” said Dogra. The two sides were looking to project a “plus moment” in their relationship, although the border dispute remains a “punctuation mark” and a source of concern for New Delhi, he said.

Another growing irritant to the relationship is around trade. China’s exports to India exceeded its imports by about $105 billion last year — an imbalance that’s more than doubled over the past decade.

“The desirable outcomes from India’s standpoint will at best be gradual,” said Shubhada Rao, an economist and founder of QuantEco Research. “Expectations of swift improvement, especially in trade dynamics, would be unrealistic. The trade balance remains extremely skewed in favor of China currently.”
India remains highly dependent on Beijing for consumer goods and for inputs for its manufacturing sector, including its massive drug-making industry.

Additionally, India is reliant on China for specialized products like rare earth magnets needed to meet its ambitious goals in the electric vehicle, renewable energy and consumer electronics sectors. Beijing has leveraged the imbalance at times, blocking specialized equipment from leaving China and recalling staff working in India.
Pankaj Mohindroo, chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association, said businesses want predictability in the China-India relationship, which has been lacking since 2020.

“The current dialog between the two governments is a highly positive step,” he said. “For global supply chains to function efficiently, industry requires smooth access to capital goods and business mobility, such as visas.”

There’s been notable steps toward closer ties since last year. China and India indicated progress in border talks in August, while India has loosened some curbs on investment from Chinese companies. Just before Xi’s touchdown in New Delhi on Saturday, China Southern Airlines announced that it will resume its daily Guangzhou-New Delhi route starting Sept. 21, ending a six-year suspension. It’s the third major Chinese carrier to restore routes.
“This situation has not come easily and needs to be cherished,” Xi said of the reset in the Saturday meeting with Modi.

Other thorny obstacles remain. Beijing’s support of Pakistan, which was involved in a brief armed conflict with India last year, remains a concern to New Delhi. Pakistan deployed Chinese fighter jets during that clash, and most recently showcased an air-defense system resembling a Chinese platform in a promotional video.
“The key would be in sustaining communication and following up from this meeting,” said Dylan Loh, associate professor at Nanyang Technological University.

items.title: A $7 Billion Gas Bill Sees Developing Asian Nations Sour on LNG
body: The loss of a fifth of liquefied natural gas supply due to the US-Iran war is blowing out costs for Asia’s developing markets, and forcing a rethink of the fuel’s long-term future in the region.

Qatari shipments of LNG through the Strait of Hormuz have all but dried up since the conflict started at the end of February. That’s deprived Asian buyers of contracted supply of the power-station and industrial fuel, pushing them into the spot market where prices are surging.

The major non-China emerging-market Asian buyers — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Thailand and Vietnam — have spent a collective $7.4 billion since the start of the war on spot LNG, according to a Bloomberg News analysis of purchase tenders. A similar amount of the fuel cost about $3.1 billion under long-term contracts over the same period last year.

The more than doubling of costs threatens to tarnish the reputation of LNG as a reliable energy source, especially as it’s just a few years after another war — between Russia and Ukraine — also led to shortages and a spike in prices. The crux of the problem is that countries need gas today, as they can’t quickly change their energy mix without risking blackouts.
Longer term, though, many of them are now looking for ways to wean themselves off LNG. Renewables like solar and wind, coal, nuclear, or locally produced gas or piped supply are some of the options.

“If prices remain at such levels, we think that LNG will have a problem competing with the alternative fuels,” Fabian Kor, the executive vice president for Asia at SEFE Marketing & Trading Ltd., a German LNG buyer, said at a conference in Singapore last week.

At stake are billions of dollars of investments in what, until this year, was the fastest-growing fossil fuel with a vital bridging role in the shift away from dirtier coal to renewables. Shell Plc, one of the top producers, said in a report in August that it expected LNG demand to rise by 65% by 2050, driven mainly by South and Southeast Asia.

Whether that’s still a realistic target will be discussed at Gastech — the world’s largest LNG industry conference — in Bangkok this week. Thailand, this year’s host, has just released a long-term energy plan that set a goal of getting a minimum of 65% of its electricity from renewables by 2050, which will come partially at the expense of natural gas.
Solar is becoming an attractive option for some developing Asian countries, especially as battery costs have come down more than 30% over the last four years.

Pakistan, once viewed as a high-growth LNG market, is likely to increase solar and hydropower generation given the direct impact of the Hormuz disruptions, said Akshay Modi, an analyst at BloombergNEF. Bangladesh, which has spent over $2 billion replacing lost Qatari LNG volumes, is rolling out incentives for consumers to install solar panels.

For Vietnam and the Philippines, it could be a case of shifting back to coal, according to BNEF’s Modi. Consumption of the dirtiest fossil fuel is set to hit a record high this year as demand is bolstered by higher gas prices and a strong El Niño that’s boosting air-conditioning use, according to the International Energy Agency.

The war in the Middle East is also forcing countries to look for alternative producers to Qatar, which supplied about 20% of the super-chilled fuel before the conflict. About 80% of LNG buyers expect to shift their procurement strategy, and prioritize geographical diversification over the next few years, according to a McKinsey & Co. survey.

That could increase the appeal of projects with direct access to Asia. TotalEnergies SE and Exxon Mobil Corp. are trying to advance Papua LNG in Papua New Guinea, with a final investment decision due later this year. The US and Canada may also benefit.

Already, years of high prices have curbed LNG adoption. Some 47 proposed gas-fired power plants — totaling $52 billion — have been canceled, withdrawn or shown no progress of moving forward over the last five years in countries including the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

“If you look back a decade ago at industry forecasts, they were saying that LNG to power was going to be the main source of demand growth,” said Sam Reynolds, research lead for LNG and gas in Asia at IEEFA. “One geopolitical conflict is a really negative thing. A second geopolitical conflict is a pattern. And that is, fundamentally, being recognized by Asian countries.”

items.title: Swedish Voters Left in Limbo for Days in Closest Ever Election
body: Sweden’s election will go down to the wire, the tightest in its history, and one that will hinge on the complete counting in coming days of late-arriving ballots and votes from overseas.

At the beginning of the night, exit polls indicated the center-left bloc was on course to reclaim power. By morning, its lead stood at three seats, still leaving open a scenario in which the governing coalition nudges ahead. A similar development occurred in 2022. At stake now is whether the far-right, long shut out, would join a government for the first time.

The opposition forces headed by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson command 176 seats versus 173 for the ruling bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson when 94% of votes had been counted. All party leaders said the result was too close to call on election night.
On Monday, the groups began internal talks as they awaited clarity.
The krona and the benchmark OMX Stockholm 30 were little changed in early trading on Monday as investors brushed aside the political turmoil.
Read More: Swedish Markets Unfazed as Election Outcome Hangs in Balance

The new deadline to look out for is Wednesday, when officials will count ballots that didn’t reach polling stations in time for election day. The tally consists mainly of advance votes cast in other municipalities over the weekend, as well as late-arriving ballots from Swedes living abroad.

The count can be extended to Thursday if necessary, according to the Swedish Election Authority, leaving the country of almost 11 million people and the Nordic’s biggest economy, home to Volvo AB and H&M AB, in an unprecedented state of uncertainty.

The late tally can be significant. In 2022, about 218,000 valid votes were added to the preliminary Riksdag result after election night, according to official data. Turnout was also down from the last election, at about 80%.
“So far, the market seems to be taking the election results in stride, even though the krona has weakened by barely one öre against the euro,” economists at lender SEB AB said in a client note.

Around 28,000 votes currently separate the blocs, public broadcaster SVT said. Four years ago, the difference between the blocs ended up being around 50,000 votes, and back then, exit polls also failed to correctly predict the winner who turned out to be Kristersson.
He refused to throw in the towel.
“Which government is going to govern Sweden in the coming years is still an open question,” Kristersson said.
Senior Social Democrat lawmakers gathered at the Social Democrats headquarters in central Stockholm for internal talks on Monday, with Party Secretary Tobias Baudin reportedly reaching out to allies.
“There will be many discussions with many parties,” Baudin said. “All parties will have to engage in some give and take,” he said.
SWEDEN INSIGHT: Election Clear as Mud, Fiscal Prudence to Stay
Kristersson said he would meet members of his Moderate Party and then the leaders of his allied parties “toward the evening.”
“We have a stable government in place now which can solve the problems we face just now, and then I will get back to you when I see a way forward,” he said.

The risk for Social Democrats, hoping to stage a comeback, is that Swedish expats tend to tack right and therefore their votes have the potential to tip the scales against the left-leaning group. In Peru, it was the diaspora that eventually gave conservative Keiko Fujimori the edge in a razor-thin election.
Speaking at her party’s election-night celebration, Andersson struck a note of cautious optimism.
“Now we will wait for the final election result,” she told supporters at the Stockholm Waterfront conference center. “Every vote that has been cast must be counted.”

She added: “It appears that it will be very close, and that means that regardless of what the final election result turns out to be, there is reason to seek a new spirit of cooperation in Swedish politics.”

This was not the speech she was hoping to give. At the start of the evening Benny Andersson of ABBA fame showed up at the Social Democrats’ headquarters to bust out a version of Mamma Mia, adapting the lyrics to her name.

Even if she prevails, this is set to be the worst result for the Social Democrats in more than a century. And even if the center-right bloc emerges on top, and Jimmie Åkesson succeeds in his goal of joining government, his Sweden Democrats suffered a drop in support and is no longer the country’s second-biggest party.

The political landscape, if anything, has become more fragmented and an election that was meant to be clarifying, a de-facto referendum on the far right, has revealed a country that is deeply split along increasingly ideological lines.
Read More: Power Eludes the Populist Who Broke Swedish Progressive Politics
Indeed, any bloc that emerges that is able to form a government, will do so with the narrowest of margins.

Any talks will be complicated and can take as long as months, given it was gains from the smaller parties on both sides of the political spectrum that buoyed their blocs, and those groups will exact their demands in the negotiations.

A victory for Kristersson, who successfully slashed crime rates during his tenure, would be a vindication of his gamble to break a long-standing taboo that had kept the rising nationalist party with neo-Nazi roots at arm’s length.
Read More: Drug-Dealing Gangs Hold Key to Swedish Vote in This Suburb

It would usher a new era in Swedish politics, one where progressive politics and a welcoming attitude to refugees had long been the norm. By giving Åkesson a formal seat at the table, Swedes can expect him to have greater say on topics ranging from immigration to foreign policy.

items.title: Trump's Drug-Price Push to Cut Access Outside US, Study Says
body: The Trump administration’s push to bring US drug spending down is a powerful incentive for pharmaceutical companies to boost prices and reduce access elsewhere in the world, a study found.

The president wants drug prices on the US Medicare federal health insurance program to match those in other wealthy countries. Yet researchers found that for about three in four drugs they studied, companies would lose more revenue in the US by charging Medicare a lower price than their total sales from the drug in the cheaper reference country used to set the new benchmark.
As a result, drugmakers might raise prices in some countries or pull out of markets altogether, according to the study published Sunday in The Lancet.

Companies have cut a slew of deals with the White House, while some are also seeking to use the US policy as leverage to raise prices elsewhere. Astellas Pharma Inc., for example, said it got a higher price for a new eye medicine in Japan this year due to concerns over Trump’s pricing policy.
Read More: Trump’s Plan to Cut Drug Prices Backfires for Patients in Europe

In Europe, some companies are scaling back plans. Biogen Inc. Chief Executive Officer Chris Viehbacher said this year the company would introduce its new postpartum depression drug Zurzuvae in only a few European countries, while Roche Holding AG said earlier this year that an as-yet-unapproved breast cancer pill might not be available to patients in its home market of Switzerland.

The company said Monday it’s committed to working with health authorities in Switzerland and elsewhere to ensure patients get access, and that it will seek approval for drugs “wherever we see a path to value recognition and can secure sustainable access for patients.”

In the study, researchers from Brigham and Women’s Hospital analyzed 195 patented medicines that made up $87.9 billion of Medicare’s spending in 2024. They estimated what the program pays for the drugs after confidential rebates and discounts, and compared that to the 19 reference countries.

Lowering the Medicare price to match would save two pilot programs the US administration is using to test the policy $11.6 billion, the research team found. But that figure shrinks to $3.3 billion if the 17 companies that made separate pricing deals with the White House get an exemption.
Nine more drugmakers struck pricing deals with the administration earlier this month, which weren’t included in the analysis.

items.title: Iran Official Blocked From UN Nuclear Meeting at US's Urging
body: A top Iranian official has been blocked from addressing the International Atomic Energy Agency’s general conference in Vienna after pressure from the US.

Mohammad Eslami, the head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, had been slated to address the United Nations nuclear watchdog on Monday before Austria denied him entry. The denial of a UN-requested sanctions waiver followed urging from the Trump administration, US IAEA Ambassador Preston Wells Griffith III confirmed at the conference.

“We could not allow” an Iranian official on the UN sanctions list to travel until the Islamic Republic provides “meaningful cooperation on nuclear safeguards,” Griffith said. “His participation would have only resulted in Iran exploiting IAEA processings for propaganda.”

Iran’s Mehr News Agency reported Saturday that Eslami had already left Tehran to attend the conference. While a lower-level Iranian representative may address the gathering later this week, the move means a top emissary from Tehran won’t be able to speak at the start of the event.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei called the move “completely unjustified” at a press conference on Monday. Iran’s IAEA Ambassador Reza Najafi said it was “politically motivated” and part of a “deeply disturbing trend” that undermines Austria’s role in facilitating international diplomacy.

Austria applied to the UN Security Council for an exemption for Eslami, but was informed “that the request had been rejected due to a lack of consensus,” the country’s foreign ministry said by email. “Entry could therefore not be permitted, in view of Austria’s international obligations.”

The move to bar Iran’s top nuclear official comes more than six months into a US and Israeli war on the Islamic Republic that Trump says is essential to prevent the country from having an atomic weapon.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright is set to use the forum to deliver a warning to Tehran, insisting that the US is unequivocal in its position that “Iran must never develop or obtain a nuclear weapon.”

“Iran must fully cooperate with the IAEA, meet its safeguards obligations, and provide the access necessary for the agency to do its job,” Wright will say, according to an administration official, who asked not to be identified discussing excerpts of the speech in advance.

Wright’s planned address follows a warning from the IAEA that the agency observed construction activity at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site suspected of housing nuclear-related activity. Trump last week cited the presence of “a little activity at Pickaxe” and warned Iran “not to get cute, because we will have to hit them very hard.”
Wright is also set to highlight the IAEA’s “founding mission,” not just the addressing of nuclear security but “delivering peaceful nuclear technology to member states.”

The appeal coincides with a Trump administration push to accelerate nuclear power to help meet surging electricity demand. In July, the US and Saudi Arabia finalized a long-sought nuclear technology-sharing deal that could allow American companies to build reactors in the kingdom.
Read More: US Signs Saudi Nuclear-Sharing Deal as Enrichment Fears Rise

“As America leads a new era of nuclear energy at home and around the world, we will prove that rapid growth and uncompromising standards go hand in hand,” Wright plans to say, according to the official. “American nuclear leadership means American technology backed by the world’s highest standards of safety, security, and nonproliferation — protecting our national interests while strengthening the competitiveness of our companies and earning the trust of our partners.”

items.title: Stocks Fall as AI Slowdown Worries Hit Chipmakers: Markets Wrap
body: A selloff in chipmakers dragged down stocks as leaders of artificial-intelligence giants proposed slowing the technology’s development, with elevated oil prices also weighing on sentiment.

The rout in powerhouses like Nvidia Corp. and Broadcom Inc. sent a semiconductor gauge down by 5.9%. The Nasdaq 100 fell 0.8%. Bank of America Corp. led losses in financial shares on chief Brian Moynihan’s trading revenue warning. Brent crude topped $105, raising concern about inflation before the Federal Reserve decision. Treasury 10-year yields hovered near 5%.

A 3,800-word missive by Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei — which was endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk — said development of the most-advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm.

Microsoft Corp.’s AI researchers have released a new set of guiding tenets that place limits on the company’s development of cutting-edge AI models. The 15,000-word manifesto boils down to five words: People matter more than AI.

President Donald Trump attacked Anthropic’s chief for urging a slowdown in AI development, intensifying his opposition to new guardrails. He blamed a “SICK conspiracy” for voter backlash on AI data centers and increased concern about frontier models and added that “the only one that is happy about it is China.”
If the latest developments push out the timing of promised AI returns, it makes sense that investors would become less enthusiastic, according to Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.
Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving Fears: Explainer

“What really happened? Surely something big enough to spook Dario, Sam, and Elon into rare agreement,” said Giuseppe Sette at Reflexivity. “Whatever it was, it was probably stopped at the last minute, just before disaster struck. With China in the race, though, we don’t expect any major slowdown.”
As for any retracement in AI stocks, Sette noted that’s simply a buying opportunity.

“Concerns on AI deployment could be a sentiment negative for the AI value chain,” said Justin Post and Nitin Bansal at Bank of America Corp. “Despite potential concerns, we continue to believe AI capacity will have strong multi-year demand.”
At HSBC, Max Kettner says calls for a slower AI buildout and resulting fears for the tech sector are “overblown.” This could actually help profitability of AI companies eventually, he said.

“Whether calls to pace advanced model development will gain traction across the industry remains uncertain, but we believe they are more aimed at shaping a regulatory framework acceptable to leading AI labs,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office. “We therefore expect AI investment to continue.”

items.title: Latest Oil Market News and Analysis for Sept. 14
body: Oil rose, with fears of a tightening market after Saudi Arabia closed a major crude pipeline pitted against signs that the US may still be seeking a diplomatic resolution with Iran.

Brent edged 1% higher to settle below $106 a barrel, after earlier rising as much as 5%, while West Texas Intermediate was around $101. The commodity initially rallied on the halt of the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which has the capacity to carry about 7 million barrels a day to the Yanbu hub on the Red Sea that has been key to bypassing the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war choked off exports from the Persian Gulf.

Some of those gains faded by midday New York time after US President Donald Trump posted a series of social media comments suggesting progress on both the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The US leader said Kyiv and Moscow had agreed not to strike energy targets and that Iran “wants to make a deal, quickly and badly.” He added the US was open to the concept of engaging with Tehran.

Iran, for its part, denied Trump’s claim, according to the country’s state-run media. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would suspend its strikes on Russian energy targets “if our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains” from further attacks on its critical infrastructure. The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Still, traders seized on the diplomatic rhetoric to unwind long positions that had become increasingly stretched. Crude’s nine-day relative strength index has been trading in overbought territory for the past week, leaving room for further downside. Trend-following commodity trading advisers are also holding at 100% maximum long in Brent, suggesting they’ve exhausted buying capacity, according to Kpler.

Investors are also assessed conflicting signals over when the Saudi pipeline would reopen. The Associated Press reported it will be out of service for several weeks, citing two regional officials. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, meanwhile, said on Monday he expects the Saudi pipeline to be up and running “very soon.” Saudi Aramco didn’t respond to earlier inquiries about how long the disruption would last.

The market impact will also depend on how much oil can be drawn from storage at Yanbu, how long it will take to get crude flowing again and how much can be rerouted by sneaking barrels through the vital energy chokepoint, the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil prices were already rallying before Monday’s barrage of news. The global benchmark moved back above $100 for the first time since July last week, as sliding inventories and rising Chinese buying tightened the market. Brent crude is up more than 75% this year.

The crisis is delivering an inflationary jolt to the global economy as the cost of natural gas and fuels also surge. After US data showed the pace of consumer price gains marched higher in August, the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates this week.

The market for oil products has been especially strained. Diesel futures are trading at around $200 a barrel, and refiners are now paying enormous premiums to secure crude as the cost of selling fuels is soaring. They’re willing to pay record amounts for ships to carry those barrels across the world, with vessel availability also incredibly scarce.

Meantime, tensions over Hormuz remain high and escalating fighting between the Houthi militant group and Saudi Arabia-backed forces has complicated matters. A meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab nations over a temporary shipping lane through the waterway was postponed, highlighting tensions with the Islamic Republic following the recent flare-up in fighting.
Wright said he was confident that flows through Hormuz will increase in the weeks ahead, and that over 12 million barrels went through the chokepoint last night.

Even before the assault on the East-West conduit, oil output from Saudi Arabia had been under pressure. Riyadh recently reported to OPEC that its crude production last month sank to the lowest level since 1990.

The kingdom’s storage at Yanbu could support exports for five to seven days, but a pipeline outage beyond that would cause “huge disruption,” said Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank Ltd. Pending clarity on repairs, the near-term path pointed toward a test of $120 a barrel, he said.

items.title: Amazon Spends More on Sports Than Netflix, YouTube Combined
body: Good evening from Toronto, where I am sitting down for a movie at the Princess of Wales Theatre.

Some exciting news for our squad: Dawn Chmielewski has joined Bloomberg as an editor on our media and entertainment team. I’ve known Dawn for most of my career and she’s one of the sharpest and kindest people on the beat.
Bloomberg just hosted its annual Power Players event in New York. My colleagues broke down the biggest takeaways here. Screentime is a couple weeks away. Lord help me.
I’m going to bring you the details from a special conversation I had at Power Players, but first…
Five things you need to know

Amazon spent more than $22 billion on entertainment programming last year, a figure that includes film, TV, music and podcasts. It’s the biggest spender on sports rights of any major technology company.

And yet, many people still struggle to understand Amazon’s strategy. They still wonder if CEO Andy Jassy will wake up one day and shut it all down. (That’s not happening when you commit to a decade-long deals with the NFL and NBA by the way.)

So at this year’s Power Players, I thought it would be a good idea to get the perspective of Jay Marine, a long-time Amazon executive who is the company’s head of sports and the person in charge of Prime Video in the US. He also oversees advertising, in case he needed more to do.
How does streaming the NFL, the NBA, NASCAR and soccer benefit a retail and cloud storage company?
Everything comes back to Prime. We want that to be the best membership program in the world.

It started off as a retail program and free shipping. But entertainment’s become a big pillar of a diverse and differentiated subscription program. Sports are uniquely valuable because they come with built-in fan bases. So it’s almost like a guaranteed hit. Customers have shown that they care about it because they’re willing to pay for it.
How big is Prime?

Hundreds of millions. We said over 200 million Prime members many years ago. On an audience basis, we’ve announced that we have over 315 million monthly viewers of Prime Video worldwide, 130 million monthly in the US.

At that scale, the things we do have to move the needle. Large, tier-one sports have proven to move the needle. They do that in a few ways. One is acquisition. They bring new members into Prime. We also see when people watch live sports, whether it’s Champions League in Europe or NFL or NBA here, they also renew their membership at a higher rate. Sports are uniquely valuable. Unfortunately, I’m not the only one who knows that, so they’re also uniquely expensive.
Ampere Analysis pegged your annual sports expenditure at $3.8 billion. Is that in the ballpark?
I don’t think we really disclosed that. You could probably piece it together though. You’re good at math. It’s significant.

Netflix has said there’s no way to make money from renting big sports packages. Many of the traditional media companies view sports as a loss leader. They spend a lot of money on sports rights and then direct those audiences to other places they can make money. Is sports something that you make money on?
When you talk about traditional networks, and I don’t want to speak on their business model, my guess is it makes sense for them.
Otherwise they wouldn’t continue to do it.

Exactly. You really have to look at the whole picture about what it’s doing. We all have different business models. When someone outbids us, I don’t say, “Oh, they overpaid.” Because I don’t know. They have a different business model. They’re trying to achieve different things.

I can only value what I think it’s worth to Amazon. That’s not an exact science. When we did an 11-year deal with the NBA, no one can predict 11 years. But we bet on that league, bet on Adam Silver and that younger audience and what it could do. So there’s always a leap of faith.

You’ve talked about how disciplined you are, but you have the NFL, which is the most expensive. You have the NBA, which was just this huge deal. What is the last thing you wanted that you had to bow out of or didn’t get?

You probably could guess because we look at everything. As long as something’s big enough and interesting to us, we look really hard at it. And then we say, “Well, this is the threshold.” There’s been lots of properties that I would love to have on Prime Video that didn’t work out or they’re just not available yet.
Do you have the portfolio right now that you want?

This will be our fifth year of Thursday Night Football. Our audience was over 15 million on average for a game last year, up 60% from year one. Going into year one, the questions were all very different than your questions now. It was like, “Is this going to work? Will people find it?”

When I used to talk to leagues back before we launched Thursday Night Football, they all wanted to talk to us and wanted us to bid, but they weren’t ready for us to win. They just wanted to scare the shit out of the other networks, which was very effective. We had to prove ourselves. But in a very short amount of time, no one asked those questions anymore. We ended up going from the risky choice to the safer choice.
I’m very happy with the portfolio. In the US, it’s 12 months of live sports – and that’s not counting international.
You have a lot of soccer outside the US. You don’t have much here. Is there interest? World Cup’s coming up, EPL’s coming up, MLS is coming up.

We look at everything. The World Cup was fantastic this past year, and I thought the broadcasters did a great job with that. That’s an incredible property. The time zone matters there, of course.  But it’s a great competition and we know international soccer or football very well. We’re looking at that for sure.
You’ve used the word fragmented to talk about the media landscape a couple times. The government and the FCC have said sports rights are too fragmented. What do you make of that criticism?
I get it. If you look at the NFL, your local game is always also on broadcast. Even Thursday Night Football, if the Lions are playing in Detroit, you can also get that on broadcast.

We’re really trying to help solve that problem. On Prime Video, we have other streaming partners who sell their subscriptions or channels all within the Prime Video app. You don’t have to leave, so it’s one login, one password. Fox One came on with their new launch. Peacock came on. Paramount Plus, which is CBS. So essentially, you can find every NFL game with the exception of Monday night within Prime Video. That includes also entertainment.

One of the best decisions we ever made was the decision to invite other merchants to let them sell on Amazon because we decided that’s the best thing for consumers. It adds selection. It makes sure you have the best pricing.

We’re doing the same thing in video because if you work backwards from customers, they want the most selection. Do they really want to download three apps and have to call their spouse to remember the password for X app? No.
Do you care if it’s an Amazon operated production or if it comes from some other company?
I have a slight preference because I like what we do on the production and innovation side. But no one company can afford all sports rights. It’s just impossible.
ESPN tried for a second.

It’s just not going to happen. And, by the way, that’s true in movies and TV. No one gets to corner the market on making a great show or movie. Once you come to that realization, you’re like, “Okay, I can’t control what other companies do anyway. Why don’t I partner and let them bring their content on our platform?”

Streaming started off as consumer-friendly. But it now has advertising. The cost of everything is going up. Are we nearing a tipping point where it’s going to be where cable was 20 years ago? Where it starts to be annoying?

There was a simplicity of cable. Go to one place and it’s got everything. The price got incredibly high as things got added and you had no choice. Canceling, you’d have to spend your whole afternoon to cancel. So there’s things that were just not customer friendly in that model. But the aggregation part, in theory, from a usability standpoint, that part worked.

You’re going to see a little bit of more of that happening on streaming. The challenge is how do you get bundles and those things to be seamless? Every company has their own approach and agenda. As you know, those are not easy deals to get done.

Amazon has been investing more in local sports. The regional sports network business has been collapsing. You’ve got more than 30 teams across different leagues. You said no one can have all the rights. So does that mean there’s no world in which Amazon just becomes the home for local sports?

It could be, but it could be that those 30 teams we have now are a mix of models. Sometimes it’s directly us, sometimes it’s an RSN, but we’re the digital home for that. We’d love to be the home of local sports, whether that means it’s all Amazon only or through partners.
We only have a couple minutes left, so I’m going to go quickly. You are named the sports media czar tomorrow, what is one thing you change?
If there’s a bidder who has a diverse subscription set that includes retail, that should be at the top of the list. You said anything!
Is the NBA season too long?

I’m biased here because we had a great first year. The league feels like it’s just right. I’ve seen the criticism on both sides. Could it shorten a little bit? Maybe. But when I look at the ratings, I don’t feel it.
What is one piece of advice you have for whoever the next WNBA commissioner is?

That league is on fire. The growth in our audience numbers, I think we’re up 60%. The young stars in that league are amazing. Is it surprising that when you have that dramatic growth over the last couple years that there’s some growing pains? No doubt. The goal of any next commissioner is: focus the narrative on the game and the incredible players and talent.
What’s your Super Bowl prediction?
I’m a Detroit guy. I think the country would like to see the Bills and the Lions in the Super Bowl. I would like to see that. I’d like to be calling plays.

Hollywood will crown its favorite TV shows Monday night at the Emmy Awards. The Pitt and Widow’s Bay are projected to capture the top prizes while their respective networks, HBO and Apple TV, are projected to dominate the evening. Netflix will place a distant third.
But which of the year’s “best” shows had the biggest impact on the business of TV?
That can be hard to answer. One key metric is whether a show attracts new customers. Widow’s Bay drove 680,000 signups to Apple TV – more than rival Hacks did for HBO, per Antenna.
Another, especially as these services prioritize advertising, is raw viewership. Widow’s Bay was the least-watched nominee in any of the major categories, per Nielsen.
The most-watched nominees are The Pitt, Abbott Elementary and The Beast in Me.
Rod Wave’s Don’t Look Down. The rapper moved the equivalent of almost 100,000 units. Alex Warren, of the hit song Ordinary, is second.
The World Cup provided a huge boost to NBCUniversal and Fox. NBCU eclipsed Disney in TV viewership during the month of July, per Nielsen.

But the real winner was YouTube. The Google-owned video site accounted for 14.2% of TV viewing in the US in July, despite the World Cup. That is a new record for the Gauge. Netflix slipped to 7.8%. We aren’t far away from YouTube being twice as big as Netflix.

items.title: Burnham Says UK Needs 'Culture Shift' to Support Risk Takers
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain needs a “culture shift” to make it easier to start companies and reward risk-taking, as he sought to quell the concerns of business leaders before next month’s budget.

The government is on the side of “people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” Burnham said ahead of a roundtable and reception with business bosses on Monday. He said the state will be a “partner for growth” and pledged to bring the model that helped boost growth rates in Greater Manchester to the rest of the country.

“If we’re going to unlock this country’s full potential, we need a culture shift in how Britain does business,” he said ahead of the event, according to a government statement. “It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business, and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.”

Retailers and banks have been among firms to warn Burnham and Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey against further tax rises to shore up the public finances at the Oct. 28 budget. The UK economy has outperformed expectations this year, with the latest figures for July suggesting that growth was fueled by firms that offer artificial intelligence products.

However, the Middle East conflict has worsened an already precarious fiscal situation, with UK government borrowing costs recently hitting their highest in decades. Healey has promised to cut through a thicket of regulation to support businesses, but may need to raise some revenue to help restore a fiscal buffer that’s likely to have been eroded by the war.

Burnham will host bosses from companies including HSBC Holdings Plc, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc, BT Group Plc, and J Sainsbury Plc, plus the founders of Octopus Energy Group Ltd. and Starling Bank Ltd. at a roundtable and reception in Downing Street on Monday.

“When local leaders have the tools to get things done and government works in partnership with business, you can pull in investment, create jobs and transform communities,” Burnham said ahead of the event. “My government will bring that same approach to the whole country and be a partner for growth to make every part of Britain better off.”

While AI is starting to fuel UK economic growth, politicians on Sunday raised concerns that governments are struggling to keep pace with the rapid advances ahead of a summit hosted by King Charles III that will bring together leaders from the sector.

Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat warned in an interview with Sky News that governments “simply do not have the speed to keep up with the advances that are happening,” after bosses from the world’s biggest AI platforms sounded the alarm over the weekend.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told Sky News that she’s “pleased that these companies are also talking about the threats as well as the opportunities,” but added that there needs to be international cooperation on the issue.

Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei said in a blog post on Saturday that the sector needed to slow down the development of the most advanced models, saying his company would introduce new safety steps. OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk quickly signaled their agreement with Amodei.

Concerns mounted last week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, warning that the sector’s leading firms were not “acting responsibly” and “gambling with our lives” in a race to develop the technology.
The King will bring together leaders from Nvidia Corp., Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI at Dumfries House in Scotland this week, the Sunday Times newspaper reported.
The UK hosted the world’s first AI safety summit in 2023. Rishi Sunak, who was prime minister at the time, warned in a piece for the Sunday Times of the risks from losing control of AI models.
“I am an AI optimist, but we can’t ignore these latest developments,” he said.

items.title: Trump Basks as Irish Open Host in Brief Break From Midterm Woes
body: President Donald Trump took center stage at the Irish Open on Sunday, reveling in a golf tournament at his family’s Doonbeg resort even as his political agenda faces a critical test in November’s midterm elections.

Just days after attending a convention in Dallas to bolster fellow Republicans confronting a tough election, Trump was an ocean away from the campaign trail, watching some of the golf world’s elite compete and personally presenting the trophy to the eventual winner, Shane Lowry.

Trump appeared to take particular pride in seeing an Irish golfer win the tournament in his home country. The president had talked up Lowry throughout his visit and was seen clapping as he played the 18th hole on Sunday to clinch his victory.
Trump said that he had wanted to “stay and watch Shane win, and he did win,” adding that the golfer had shown he could “handle pressure.”

And in a surprise announcement, that drew a roar from the crowd, Trump said during the trophy ceremony that he would remove US tariffs on Irish whiskey — delivering a major trade win to Ireland. Trump credited both Lowry and Irish Prime Minister Taoiseach Micheal Martin for the move, saying they had personally lobbied him during his trip.

The trophy celebration capped a whirlwind two-day visit to Ireland funded by US taxpayers. And while Trump met Martin and President Catherine Connolly, in Dublin, the Open in the west of Ireland dominated his time.

The US president received a rapturous reception from the Doonbeg crowd, walking out Sunday to cheers and applause — a respite from protests elsewhere in Ireland and a break, albeit brief, from a perilous political climate at home.

“Welcome to Ireland, Donald,” one spectator shouted as the president stepped yards away from the first tee on Sunday. Later, as Trump watched, a group of children tried to get his attention, yelling hello at the president. At the trophy ceremony, while some boos were initially heard for Martin, Trump walked up to chants of “USA” and pumped his fist.

Trump has regularly attended high-profile sporting events. Still, the images of him going to a golf tournament in the throes of a midterm race — and just after telling his party faithful he’d campaign more vigorously — threaten to stir doubts about his focus on the election. Past pledges to campaign more aggressively failed to materialize and the president has devoted much of his time — an invaluable resource in Washington — to projects such as a White House ballroom.

Trump’s approval ratings are at record lows with voters unhappy over high consumer costs and the war with Iran. At the convention, he urged voters to act as if he were on the ballot, pointing to his administration’s immigration policy and tax breaks thus far, and pledged a $5,000 dividend for Americans if Republicans hold the House and Senate. With a price tag well over $1 trillion at a time when US public debt is already massive, the proposal was met with bipartisan skepticism over whether it could or should become law.

But Trump also undercut his own efforts, offering a tacit acknowledgement in a Fox News interview that Democrats are likely to control at least one chamber, a result that would hamper his agenda and subject his administration and family to investigations. Less than two months to Election Day, there are worries it may be too late to alter Republicans’ trajectory.
Read more: Trump’s Two Days in Dallas: $5,000 Cash, ‘Socialists’ and Opera

Asked about the impact of having a US president at the tournament, Northern Irish golfer Rory McIlroy, who won it last year, called it “a good thing,” noting that Trump’s presence “brings more eyeballs to the Irish Open.”
Trump walked out Sunday wearing a white “USA” hat and navy suit, and watched as both Jacob Skov Olesen, a Danish golfer, and Lowry began their final rounds.

After Lowry started his round, Trump took questions from reporters that touched on Ukraine, the Federal Reserve, AI regulation and other matters, but seemed most animated when talking about the tournament.

Asked which golfer at the Open he’d like to play with, Trump said: “Well, right now I’ll take Shane, and I’ll also take Rory, and I’ll also take about 40 others because you know what, they’re great players. They’re all great. Every one of them. It’s amazing.”
Earlier: Trump’s Ireland Visit Puts Dublin’s Charm Strategy to the Test
Trump’s trip to Ireland was also the latest demonstration of how his public duties often mix with his personal interests.

While not a state visit, Trump received a red carpet and honor guard in Dublin, delicate diplomacy from Irish leaders even as polls show he is deeply unpopular in that country. Thousands protested Trump’s visit in Dublin on Saturday.

Trump in a speech to business leaders jabbed at Ireland and Europe broadly over trade, regulation and immigration. And he waded into further controversy by saying he would love to see a unified Ireland. But Irish leaders will likely be pleased with the results of their charm offensive.
Motorcades whisked the president to his Dublin meetings. By midday Saturday, Trump was flying off to Doonbeg, shifting the spotlight on a major property for his family’s business.

The Irish Open was held at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in County Clare for the first time, highlighting how the president’s family has long pushed to host high-profile tournaments at their properties. The course, known for its sandy dunes and ocean views, was designed by legendary golfer Greg Norman and opened in 2002, with the lodge following in 2006.

It’s become a key economic driver in Ireland’s rural west. Trump bought the property in 2014, rebranding the estate, in a deal he’s said in interviews took just hours. Doonbeg, a village of almost 300, has welcomed the tourism that brings American golfing enthusiasts to the town.

items.title: CFOs Face a Tougher Call on When to Borrow (ASAN, TOBA)
body: Welcome to CFO Briefing, a newsletter dedicated to corporate finance and what leaders need to know. This week, I take a closer look at the current state of the credit markets and talk to CFOs about the upcoming Fed meeting. We also have an interview with Mozilla’s Eric Muhlheim.
It’s been a good year for CFOs looking to borrow. Credit markets have largely remained open despite the war in Iran, spreads have been low and investors have been eager to buy.

Finding the right time to sell debt may soon become more difficult. High energy prices are driving up inflation and interest rate expectations ahead of the US midterm elections in November, essentially shortening the window for executives to this month and October.
With 10-year Treasury yields approaching 5% and the government buying back debt, companies are weighing whether to tap investors now, or wait in hopes of lower rates further down the road.

That hope might prove elusive, as bond traders are pricing in about a 90% chance of a rate increase when the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee meets Sept. 15-16. Europe has already moved in that direction, with the European Central Bank lifting its deposit rate to 2.5% and potentially more hikes to come.

Issuers are “confused about the intervention in the Treasury market, perplexed about what’s going to happen with rates and a little skittish about the elections,” said Anna Pinedo, a capital markets partner at Mayer Brown who advises corporate issuers on debt offerings.

Recent changes in short- and medium-term Treasury rates have had a chilling effect on some companies, said Amol Dhargalkar, chairman of financial-services firm Chatham Financial. “Clients are sitting tight and hoping that this is a momentary challenge for the bond market rather than a fundamental repricing of risk,” he said.

Still, activity has been buoyant since the Labor Day holiday. US investment-grade bond sales are coming off three record months and notched nearly $68 billion of issuance during the past week, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Companies sold $12 billion in junk bonds since Labor Day, the most since early June, and also tapped the leveraged loan markets.
Asana, a San Francisco-based software company, decided not to wait and started talking to banks about replacing a term loan due in November with a new credit facility.

“There is access to capital and a willingness to underwrite and put money to work,” said Aziz Megji, the company’s chief financial officer, adding that market conditions are noticeably different from a few months ago when there was widespread investor skepticism around lending to software-as-a-service businesses.
“Six to nine months ago, you would try to get a conversation with a large institution and it would be very difficult,” he said.
Finance chiefs outside the US are watching the same dynamics. Juli Oktarina, the CFO of Indonesian energy firm TBS, said she’s monitoring US funding costs closely.

Jakarta-based TBS recently refinanced a S$385 million ($303 million) loan with a syndicate of nine international banks and gained shareholder approval for a rights issue earlier this year. “Fed rates are very applicable to us,” Oktarina said, adding that the company weighs different options to meet its financing needs.

At the same time, US companies are increasingly seeking overseas investors, with Amazon recently selling its first bonds in the UK and Alphabet doing the same in Australia. After Labor Day, six American issuers tapped European investors in a single day — a first, based on the data compiled by Bloomberg. “You are seeing much more funding diversification across geographies, across investor bases and structures,” said Mayer Brown’s Pinedo.
And, in another first, risk premiums on emerging-market corporate debt indexes are converging with comparable US benchmarks, signaling that traditional boundaries between those markets are blurring.

Yet there are questions about how long the current conditions can last. Recent deal sizes, investors’ ability to absorb them and questions about when AI-related investment will generate sufficient revenues all play into that. With issuance after issuance, investors may be approaching a tipping point. “I think sentiment could be starting to turn,” Pinedo said.

Mozilla, known for its Firefox web browser and the Mozilla VPN, has set itself no lesser goal than to further the health of the internet. That mission is particularly relevant as artificial intelligence changes the way the internet works and how people use it. The software firm — which is a subsidiary of Mozilla.org, a nonprofit that promotes openness, innovation and participation on the internet — recently appointed a new chief executive to help revamp its strategy. Eric Muhlheim, who became CFO in 2021 after stints at Buzzfeed and Disney, talks about balancing mission and returns, diversifying Mozilla’s revenue streams and AI costs. His answers have been edited for length and clarity.
How would you describe the current operating environment?

We’re in another industrial revolution that transforms the nature of knowledge work. That can be an incredibly confusing time for everybody. There’s a lot of excitement about AI, and people lose sight of the fact that it is another tool that’s eventually meant to make people more productive. It just drastically transforms the way we do work, and it’s going to transform the nature of the internet. But at the end of the day, you still have people as the end point.
How do you weigh the financial interests of shareholders and the company’s mission more broadly?

That makes the [CFO job] a little trickier. If we were a company that was solely focused on making money, it would be fairly easy because the trade-offs would only be aimed in one direction. We have to make trade-offs in both directions. We want to make sure that we can fulfill the mission of the company, but we need to do that sustainably. We have to generate a certain profit that is not only used to invest in our browser and our software, but we take a portion of that profit and send it back to the [Mozilla foundation], which invests in projects across open source and distributed AI so that we can create conditions where there aren’t monopolies.
How are you diversifying the company’s revenue streams?

One of the aspects is focusing on advertising inside the browser. It’s going to be privacy-preserving. It’s not going to focus on the kind of surveillance capitalism that fuels the entire advertising economy on the internet. There are definitely challenges in doing that, I am not going to lie about that. We’re also focused on other areas – one of them is Firefox Enterprise, which addresses corporate customers. Firefox has always been used by organizations, but we can provide more value for them with a stronger offering for enterprises.
You changed how the company manages its reserves. What drove that?

That is part of why I came in about five years ago. We did a big review of our overall investment policy and moved from a more conservative approach to one that is more aligned with nonprofit endowments where you are investing for both security and total return of those assets. By changing our overall investment policy, we have been able to take advantage of the returns in the market. A lot of that money is going to the investments that [the Mozilla foundation] is making.
How are you keeping AI costs in check?

So rather than thinking about AI as an entirely different line item, we’re seeing it as a trade-off between capital and labor. Spending has gone up. It is quite a bit higher than we thought it was going to be. We budget for a certain amount of headcount, we budget for a certain amount of other tools, and if AI ends up being the more productive line item to increase rather than people or other software, then we will make the trade-offs. My goal this year has been to hold people to their overall departmental budgets and then give them control. As we get to the end of the year, it’s obvious that managers need to have visibility into how they’re using AI so they can make informed choices about what they do. We also need to invest centrally in AI governance.
GoldenTree Asset Management named Ellen Conti as CFO. She joins from Sculptor Capital, where she was CFO and executive managing director.
ElevenLabs appointed Ethan Tandowsky as CFO. He previously held the same role at payments firm Adyen.
CME Group promoted Jack Tobin, its chief accounting officer since 2015, to the CFO role, effective in March.
Lyft named Michael Brous as CFO, succeeding Erin Brewer, who is retiring.
Polymarket appointed Warren Jenson as its first CFO as the prediction-market operator expands in the US.
HSBC said CFO Pam Kaur will step down next year.
Glanbia named Wendy Chang Smith as CFO-designate, succeeding Mark Garvey, who will retire after 13 years as finance chief. Chang Smith is set to become CFO on March 31, 2027.

items.title: Hormuz Meeting With Iran and Gulf Nations Delayed, Oman Says
body: A planned meeting for Monday between Iran and several Gulf nations on creating a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed, according to Oman’s foreign minister.
Badr Albusaidi said in a post on X that the meeting is being delayed “in the interests of consensus,” without offering any details about next steps.

The meeting was put off to ensure “appropriate conditions for a constructive dialogue that contributes to achieving sustainable understandings supporting the region’s security and stability,” Oman’s Foreign Ministry added in a post on X.
Iran said the meeting of foreign ministers was postponed at the request of regional countries, according to the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency.
Tehran had planned to formally unveil a deal on the shipping lane after a flurry of diplomatic activity including a rare meeting between senior officials from Tehran and Abu Dhabi.

In the days ahead of the planned meeting, it wasn’t clear which nations would attend. Bahrain had ruled out participating, citing recent Iranian-backed attacks on Gulf sites, while escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed forces and the Houthis, a group based in neighboring Yemen and supported by Iran, was also complicating the plans.

Tehran had indicated any deal wouldn’t amount to a full reopening and it would still decide on which ships could cross the strait. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the proposed meeting as an “important event” and a step toward building trust, in an interview with Al Araby Al Jadid.

Negotiations on details such as the fees ships may be charged were set to continue between Iran and Oman later, according to people familiar with the talks, who asked not to be identified discussing private deliberations.

Brent crude prices have topped $105 a barrel in recent days as renewed Middle Eastern tensions heightened concerns about global supplies. Soaring prices at the pumps pose a problem for President Donald Trump’s Republican Party with just over 50 days to go before midterm elections.
Asked earlier Sunday about a possible meeting of Gulf nations with Iran, Trump told reporters, “I don’t care. That’s up to them. That’s fine.”

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright had also downplayed the chances of a Hormuz deal during an interview Sunday. He said markets will need to continue relying on transit that he estimates is supplying 10 million barrels a day of crude and oil products through the Strait of Hormuz.

Together with bypass pipelines, that means “we’re back to two-thirds or north of two-thirds of the previous flows,” Wright said. “So the world oil markets are tighter than we’d like today, but they’re not overly tight.”
Read More: US Energy Chief Downplays Chance of Hormuz Advance With Iran

The US and Iran exchanged strikes on oil tankers in the Persian Gulf earlier this month. Tensions flared again in the strait over the weekend, with UK Maritime Trade Operations saying Sunday a fire broke out on a ship hit by a projectile the day before.
Iran’s state-run IRIB reported an “enemy strike” on a commercial vessel off Iran’s Qeshm and Hengam islands that killed one person.

Saudi Aramco shares fell nearly 1.1% on Sunday to their lowest level since March, after the kingdom closed its East-West pipeline, a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for its oil exports, due to drone attacks by Iraq-based militants.
