items.title: A 5% Treasury Yield Raises New Risks for Markets, Economy
body: The bond selloff has driven a key Treasury yield to the verge of 5%, worsening angst from Wall Street to Washington about higher borrowing costs hitting the US economy.

After surging oil prices threatened to deliver a fresh inflation shock and the Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to ease the pressure on the government debt market, the benchmark 10-year yield jumped to 4.97% by the end of last week. That’s just shy of the peak in October 2023, when it climbed over 5% briefly during a single trading session, before coming back down as buyers rushed in.

The recent rout has increased the stakes for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh going into the central bank’s meeting on Wednesday. The market steadied on Friday only after data showed a stronger-than-expected rise in consumer prices last month, strengthening speculation that policymakers will start raising interest rates to tame inflation that’s exceeded its target for half a decade.
“The Fed is behind the curve, definitely,” said Tracy Chen, a portfolio manager with Brandywine Global Asset Management. “Yields are heading higher in the medium-term.”

She said that’s because some of the factors pushing longer-term yields higher, like the inflationary impacts of the Iran war, aren’t in policymakers’ control. “How high I don’t know, but I think definitely beyond 5%.”

Bond yields have been rising globally since President Donald Trump launched his war on Iran in late February, disrupting the supply of Middle Eastern oil and gas. In the US, the artificial-intelligence boom, which is both flooding markets with debt and pouring stimulus into the economy, and concerns about the federal government’s swelling deficit have also played a role.
The upward move has vexed Trump as it ripples through markets, driving up the cost of mortgages and other loans ahead of the mid-term elections in November.

Early this month, he threatened to cut off all US trade with some countries if the Fed didn’t reduce interest rates, a step that would almost certainly worsen the selloff by fanning inflation fears. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to restrain the rise in bond yields by increasing the department’s debt buybacks, only to see them spike last week after his first such operation underwhelmed investors.

With little progress toward ending the conflict in the Middle East, investors are bracing for the risk that the bond-market rout will continue. Ian Lyngen, head of US rates strategy at BMO Capital Markets, said he’s anticipating that 10-year yields will breach 5% “in very short order.”

There’s nothing inherently significant about crossing that level, which it hasn’t closed above since 2007. But such round numbers are often seized on as key pivot points that can catalyze decisions by investors and policymakers.

Treasury yields are particularly important because they serve as a baseline for other loans. In the stock market, they’re also used as a discount rate to gauge the present value of profits expected in the years ahead. The more yields rise, the smaller those earnings look.

Some investors say that could start exerting a drag on stocks, which have been hovering near record highs because of the strong profits thrown off by the AI boom and the resilience in the economy. Moreover, elevated bond yields could trigger a shift away from equities as investors are lured into bonds by the higher payouts.

“If you saw bond yields move to the 5% or 5.25% level I think that’s where you will see some indigestion from the equity market,” said Grace Peters, global head of investment strategy at JPMorgan Chase Private Bank. “5% psychologically has an impact.”
The turmoil of the past week — when two-yield Treasury yields saw the biggest one-day jump since Trump’s April 2025 tariffs sent markets into a tailspin — has increased pressure on the Fed.

That’s because some of the selling in recent months has been stoked by questions about Warsh, who used his first post-meeting press conference in June to drive home a message that he was focused on getting inflation back to the central bank’s 2% target. But after the meeting in July, when the Fed again kept rates unchanged, traders dumped longer-dated bonds on doubts about whether he’d follow through.

On Friday, after the Labor Department reported a larger-than-expected jump in a core inflation measure, traders wagered that it would likely force the Fed’s hand. Futures started pricing in a roughly 90% chance that it will raise its overnight benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point after the upcoming meeting.
US Treasuries steadied on Monday despite continued losses in European and UK bonds. The US two-year yield held at 4.63% in the London session, while the 10-year rate was slightly up at 4.96%.

“The more that the Fed can show its inflation fighting credibility, the more likely it’ll compress the risk premium on the back end of the Treasury curve over the medium term,” said Daleep Singh, chief global economist at PGIM Credit.

Even so, some of the other forces that have been pushing up yields are continuing unabated. The federal deficit hit $2 trillion during the first 11 months of the fiscal year. And last week Trump raised the prospect of spending more than $1 trillion by sending out $5,000 checks to every American adult if Republicans keep control of Congress after the upcoming elections, which the White House’s economic adviser said was a “serious proposal.” The conflict in the Middle East has also escalated, sending oil prices to a four-month high.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategists led by Jay Barry said they see a rate hike as likely this week, but “skew bearishly” toward long-end Treasuries due to the ways traders could react to the Fed’s statement and Warsh’s press conference. Others echoed the caution, seeing risks that the selloff could resume if the Fed surprises investors.
“The selloff in the long end, if the Fed does not hike, could potentially become much more disorderly,” said Ed Al-Hussainy, a portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle.

items.title: Indonesia's Green Fuel Boom Is Incinerating the Rainforest
body: Here’s a rare success story from Asia’s post-Hormuz energy crisis: Indonesia has managed to use biofuels to end its dependence on imported diesel. And here’s the dark side: The same policy may be exporting even more choking smoke to its neighbors.

The reason is palm oil. About a fifth of global production this year will be burned in an Indonesian engine. A government mandate requires a 50% biofuel blend in diesel, mainly used in trucks and small back-up generators.

That has helped one of the world’s biggest oil importers ride out the effects of the Iran war. In his initial response to the conflict, President Prabowo Subianto accelerated a shift from 40% to the current 50% level. That decision ended diesel imports and is saving the country $9.5 billion a year, he said last month.

The policy, however, is raising the value of a commodity intimately linked to the pall of haze currently descending across tens of millions of people in Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Indonesia itself. Electrifying the country’s truck fleet would provide the same energy security with far less cost to the environment and human health.

Burning forest lands to clear acreage for palm oil plantations is nothing new in Indonesia, and the resulting pollution has been a problem for decades. But with more than 200,000 hectares burned by August and the worst weeks still ahead, this wildfire season could be Indonesia’s most severe since 2015.

That episode caused $16 billion of economic losses and more than 100,000 premature deaths, and prompted Jakarta to tighten up its approach to forest protection. In Europe, it bolstered an anti-palm oil campaign that eventually prompted the European Union to stop classifying palm biodiesel as renewable, cutting consumption. Indonesia stabilized the resulting glut by gradually raising its blending mandate to the current level.

You can paint this as either a positive or negative story, because palm has a Jekyll-and-Hyde quality. From an established plantation, lifecycle emissions can be roughly half those of diesel. But clear rainforest or drain peat to grow it and the picture grows darker: Emissions can be twice as high as from fossil fuels.

Whether Indonesia's biofuel push helps or harms the climate, therefore, depends overwhelmingly on where the extra biofuel comes from. The government only sees the positive side of the story, arguing that all the growth in demand can be met by improving the productivity of long-established plantations and planting on degraded land.

The data suggests otherwise. Every bit of the country’s palm-oil production growth since 2015 has come from putting more land under cultivation. Palm oil acreage is up 65%, while yields have actually fallen 7%.

“Degraded land” is also a slippery term. A 2024 study found that more than half of Indonesia's palm estate was in areas that had been old-growth forest in 1990. Most wasn't converted immediately to palm. Today's rainforest can become tomorrow's fire-front, then degraded scrub and eventually a “sustainable” plantation. While international standards attempt to prevent that practice, Indonesia’s domestic rules are far looser. As a result, the passage of time can effectively  launder deforestation. Nor is there much mystery about who starts the fires. Local officials say almost all are caused by humans, and 80% of burnt land ends up as plantations.

Conditions this year are particularly combustible. The hot, dry weather brought by the current super-El Niño means infernos will burn longer and further. Crude oil has hit $100 a barrel and US diesel is at record levels, so hectares capable of growing a substitute are more valuable than ever. With tinder-dry undergrowth everywhere, the only upfront investment needed is a match.

Prabowo’s rhetoric, combining ongoing promises of protection with a vow to open up millions of hectares of woodlands for food and ethanol biofuel, also muddies the anti-deforestation message. His plan to increase the blending rate to 60% as soon as next year adds a further accelerant: It would require about 23 million metric tons of palm oil each year, an increase of a third relative to current levels.

There’s a better way to zero out diesel import dependence: Eliminate truck engines altogether. Look at the example of the world’s biggest fuel importer, China. It has already bought roughly a million electric trucks, equivalent to about one-sixth of Indonesia’s commercial vehicle fleet. The energy to power them comes overwhelmingly from domestic sources.

The islands of Java, Sumatra and Borneo are rich in generation opportunities, but they're being squandered. Putting just 10% of the palm estate under solar panels would generate enough electricity to power all of Southeast Asia, plus Japan. Only about a quarter of the country’s hydroelectric potential is being exploited. Electric vehicles already comprise nearly a quarter of car sales, but trucks and two-wheelers, hampered by inconsistent or non-existent policy support, are badly lagging.

Indonesia has found one way to escape reliance on imported diesel. China is demonstrating a better one, which can preserve both the balance of payments and the landscape. Electrification can even reduce the noxious pollution from burning land and exhaust fumes, a plague that’s reducing the health and life expectancy of millions across Southeast Asia. There’s a grand bargain out there, if only Prabowo could seize it.

items.title: Sweden's Election Race Tightens After Center-Left's Strong Start
body: Sweden’s Social Democrat-led bloc lost its early lead in a tightening election that has become a de-facto referendum on whether the far right can be kept out of power.

The four-party bloc led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson had just one parliament seat more than the incumbent government of Ulf Kristersson and his allies, according to a projection by national broadcaster SVT, at 175 versus 174 seats. Initial exit polls had given them the lead.

Kristersson’s allies, the Sweden Democrats, dropped to third place in one of the biggest surprises of the night. The party has increased its share of voters in every election to become Sweden’s second-biggest party in 2022. This is the first time it’s suffered a dip in support.
The premier’s commitment to allow the anti-immigrant Sweden Democrats into a future government and potentially offer its leader Jimmie Åkesson a key ministerial role appears to have backfired.

For many liberal Swedes, given their long history of progressive social values and tolerant attitudes to refugees, imagining the far-right party as part of a ruling coalition seems to have been a step too far.
Read More: Drug-Dealing Gangs Hold Key to Swedish Election in This Suburb
Four years ago, exit polls by SVT and TV4 failed to correctly predict the winner.
While Andersson had a comfortable lead in the months before the election, the race had tightened in the final weeks of the campaign.

“As it looks now we have a good chance to form a new government,” said Fredrik Olovsson, the Social Democrats’ energy spokesperson, at the party’s election night event in Stockholm, before the projections had been published.
Read More: Power Eludes the Populist Who Broke Swedish Progressive Politics
Mattias Karlsson, one of Åkesson’s key lieutenants over the past two decades, told Bloomberg that “right now it looks like forming a government will be very difficult.”

The election comes against a backdrop of economic weakness, with scant growth over the past four years while home values have yet to rebound from a rapid slump in 2022 to 2024. That’s brought little improvement in household finances over the past years.

While prospects for the economy are brightening and the inflation rate remains low, the labor market is recovering more slowly and the krona remains the year’s worst performer against the euro in the G10 space of major currencies.

items.title: Anthropic Said to Choose Nasdaq for Much-Anticipated IPO
body: Anthropic PBC has picked Nasdaq as its listing venue ahead of a potential record-setting initial public offering, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The Claude chatbot maker is seeking to raise as much as or more than SpaceX in an IPO that could take place as soon as October, people familiar with the preparations have said.

A Nasdaq listing would mark another win for the company this year with four of the largest US IPOs taking place on the exchange, including SpaceX’s record-setting $86.3 billion offering in June. SK Hynix Inc. followed a few weeks later after it raised $26.5 billion in an July debut.
Business Insider reported earlier on Anthropic’s choice of Nasdaq. Anthropic and Nasdaq declined to comment.

Anthropic’s IPO preparations came as OpenAI Inc. CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Elon Musk on Saturday all voiced the need to slow the pace of AI development due to escalating risks from the technology. Altman told Fortune in an interview that his company won’t go public this year, citing safety concerns.
Anthropic was set to finalize a $15 billion revolving credit facility earlier this month, Bloomberg News reported.

The AI race has fired up the IPO market, with US listings this year raising $160.6 billion, excluding blank-check firms and other financial vehicles, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That’s the most raised in a year since 2021, the data show.
Anthropic is on track to generate annualized revenue of over $65 billion based on its current performance, up more than sevenfold from its pace at the end of last year, Bloomberg News reported.

items.title: Yen Rally: Bessent Doubles Down on House of the Rising Sun
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent describes himself as the top US bond salesman. He's rapidly becoming the top Japan salesman, as well. Not only does he profess to know what that country's central bank will do, he insists that anyone wanting to bet against a sustained yen rally should try him. Bravado aside, he is on to something.

The Bank of Japan, widely expected to raise interest rates this week, is a critical player in determining the yen's trajectory. But, absent a surprise on Friday, when the authority announces its decision, it may not be the most decisive factor. What's key is the message that American muscle stands behind the yen — that Japan is not alone, for now.

The yen is enjoying a notable rally, encouraged by Bessent’s move in late July to join Tokyo in a rare intervention in the foreign-exchange market. Last week, it neared 152 to the dollar, the strongest since February. The currency certainly has room to appreciate; it had dropped to the weakest in decades, to almost 164 in July, and solo efforts by Japan to stem the retreat had negligible effect. Bessent has positioned himself as a vital player in this maneuvering. But he has also left himself open to shouldering at least part of the blame when the rally stalls. With the yen up by around 4% this month alone, further gains will likely be more modest.

There's little diplomacy in his language, despite the bilateral nature of the endeavor. “I am the house now, so when we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan is going to do,” Bessent said last week. “You can bet against me if you want.” He must know that no trade is risk free, even if it goes the way he and his counterpart, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, desire. The FX market is massive, with daily turnover of $9.6 trillion. Not even the mightiest official can fight that for very long. One of the main tasks of intervention, according to Robert Rubin, who sat in Bessent's chair during the Clinton years, is to shift psychology.

So how important is the BOJ decision? A 25-basis-point hike is now nailed on. Six weeks ago, Governor Kazuo Ueda flubbed an attempt to signal a more hawkish stance with tweaked guidance pointing to the upside risks to prices, but couched it in such language that few seemed to immediately understand it.

But things have changed. While the common view appears to be that America is strongarming a cautious BOJ, don’t be so sure. We have long argued that what was needed to strengthen the yen was not a narrowing of the yield gap with the US (that happened a long time ago), but a change in the narrative: The yen consistently weakened because it was expected to, and explanations like Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s supposedly irresponsible spending plans were always post-facto.

Bessent has seized the narrative — and he is a far better communicator than anyone in Japan. His hints have spooked yen bears. Instead of having to signal more rate increases, Ueda may merely need to play along with a hawkish hint. Markets will now be primed for this, instead of having to search for it. (One minor irony: It’s interesting that complaints about Takaichi’s alleged interference in BOJ autonomy don’t seem to be matched by grumbles about Bessent’s.)

And US involvement has focused market attention on other developments that bring money to Japan, too. The powerful Government Pension Investment Fund seems almost certain to increase its exposure to domestic bonds and indeed may already be doing so; Norway’s sovereign wealth fund has already announced plans to increase its allocation to Japanese bonds.
The risk is what happens from here: The Takaichi government fears an overly weak yen, but likes it just fine at around 150. That does not appear to be Bessent’s stance.

As for Ueda, he doesn’t have many hikes left before Japan reaches the neutral rate, believed to be around 1.5% or 1.75%. The economy has so far proven to be far more resilient to higher rates than many, ourselves included, had guessed. Past incremental rate hikes were disastrous, but rates at 1% are nonetheless still accommodative.

While Bessent was full of praise for the Japanese economy at the recent G20 meeting — he noted that while “in 2011, Japan was written off as dead, now I think it’s one of the most vibrant economies in the world” — it’s not doing so well that it needs it needs rates high enough to curb activity.

Bessent might be too confident. Rubin, who like Bessent made a fortune in finance before entering public service, liked to say that no outcome in trading is certain. It's a game of probability, and you can help shape the outcome by being firm. Rubin, for example, almost never altered his language on the strong dollar, even when coming to the aid of allies meant selling a few greenbacks.
Underlying fundamentals will have the last say. Bessent and Katayama have, at least, made Japan pessimists think twice. That’s no small thing.More From Bloomberg Opinion:

items.title: Trump Says He Will Eliminate US Tariffs on Irish Whiskey
body: Supply Lines is a daily newsletter that tracks global trade. Sign up here.
President Donald Trump said he would remove US tariffs on Irish whiskey, announcing the move Sunday while attending a golf tournament at his family’s course in western Ireland.
“On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off,” Trump said to cheers from the crowd at the Irish Open’s trophy celebration.
Irish whiskey and other goods from the European Union are generally subject to a 10% tariff under an adjusted rate following a Supreme Court ruling striking down earlier Trump levies.

Trump’s decision was announced as Shane Lowry, a professional Irish golfer, won the Open in his home country. The declaration delivers a major victory to the Irish government and highlights the often shifting — and personal — approach to trade policy under the US president. Trump has regularly turned to tariffs to push for concessions and punish nations that have bucked his interests; he has also eased levies to reward allies.

The decision, which Trump announced to roaring applause at his family’s golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, came at the end of a two-day visit marked by the country’s efforts to engage in delicate diplomacy and maintain warm relations with the US president.

Unlike other European nations that have been targets for Trump and drew his criticism this weekend, Ireland generally has been able to avoid some of that fire. Still, trade issues have been a major flashpoint between Washington and Dublin, with Trump critical of Ireland’s economic model that has attracted US companies and drawn hefty tax revenues.

The Irish Whiskey Association “heartily welcomes” the news, Irish Whiskey Association Director Eoin Ó Cáitín said in a statement. “We will continue to work with our EU and US counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero arrangement for all drinks exports.”

Ireland’s leaders rolled out the red carpet for Trump, treating him to pomp and pageantry even though he was not making an official state visit to the country. Trump was given gifts and treated to an honor guard as part of a charm offensive in Dublin on Saturday when he met with the president and prime minister.

Irish distillers had lobbied for a reduction in the duties. While whiskey distilled in the Republic of Ireland and imported into the US has been subject to the 10% tariff, Scotch as well as whiskey produced in Northern Ireland currently does not face such levies as it benefits from the US-UK trade deal.

On Sunday, Trump said he was besieged by requests to address the Irish whiskey levies during his short visit, including appeals from Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and Lowry. The Taoiseach raised the issue of tariffs on Irish whiskey with Trump when they spoke Saturday in Dublin, according to a person familiar with the matter.

“Following President Trump’s earlier action to remove tariffs on Scotch and all other UK whiskies, this announcement is another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade,” Distilled Spirits Council of the United States Chief Executive Officer Chris Swonger said in a statement.

The move will be a boost for Irish whiskey producers. The global Irish whiskey market faced a “challenging year,” especially in the US, where Irish whiskey exports declined by 5% in 2025, according to Bord Bia, the Irish food board.

Tariffs had dealt another blow to the whiskey distillers, one of Ireland’s largest and most historic indigenous industries. They had already been beset by oversupply, faltering US demand and the soaring cost of everything from energy to labor.
Wine and spirits have frequently been caught in trade disputes since Trump was sworn into his second term in the White House.

After Trump imposed tariffs on steel and aluminum last year, the EU prepared a host of retaliatory levies, including one that targeted American whiskey; Trump, in turn, threatened to slap a 200% import tax on champagnes from France. A tit-for-tat trade spat between the US and Canada also has seen provinces pulling American alcohol from store shelves.

Trump’s Irish visit was not without controversy. The president in remarks Saturday said he would like to see a unified Ireland — comments that sparked blowback in Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK.
Trump defended those remarks Sunday, calling them “fairly routine” and saying that he was only sharing “my opinion.”

items.title: Chicago Mayor Seeks Reelection in Test of Progressive Clout
body: Brandon Johnson will seek a second term as mayor of Chicago, beginning a potentially uphill battle to stay in office after his opponents have already raised millions ahead of next year’s race.

Ending months of speculation, Johnson announced the bid by video on social media and later made it official at a rally Sunday afternoon on the city’s South Side that was attended by local politicians, faith leaders and progressive organizers.

“This is what power looks like when working people organize,” he said. “Let me be clear, we are building something bigger than one organization. This is bigger than one campaign, and certainly is bigger than one individual.”

The campaign is shaping up as a bellwether for the direction of the Democratic party after a term in which Johnson’s left-wing politics roiled the Chicago business community. The race will determine whether the third-largest US city will be controlled by progressives, represented by Johnson, or a large field of more moderate, pro-business members of the party.

Johnson and other candidates have a slew of challenges to address during the campaign, including financial instability hampering the city’s budget and pensions as well as concerns about high taxes, cost of living and public safety.

While Johnson — a former Chicago Public Schools teacher and union organizer — isn’t a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, his policy platform has focused on addressing income inequality and raising taxes on millionaires and billionaires. But he has struggled to capitalize on the momentum that brought him into office when he upset incumbent Mayor Lori Lightfoot in 2023.
Read More: Chicago Mayor Race Heats Up as Democrats Eye Johnson Ouster
“When people talk about taxing the rich, that’s not a theory, that’s something we actually did here in Chicago,” he said, without citing specifics.

The mayor touted the city’s resistance to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, an executive order he signed recently that puts additional limits on data center development and a sharp drop in homicides during his tenure.
“Not only did we stand up to Donald Trump, but we set the standard for the rest of the country,” he said. “As long as I’m mayor of the City of Chicago, we will never submit to authoritarianism.”

Johnson, 50, has faced difficulty in enacting his “tax the rich” agenda. He sought a ballot referendum that would increase real estate transfer taxes on properties valued at more than $1 million, but the effort failed. A poll released in July by the Mansueto Institute for Urban Innovation at the University of Chicago gave Johnson a 23% approval rating, and only about 14% of those polled said they would like to see him seek a second term.

Chicago’s nonpartisan municipal elections have led to upsets in the past for long-shot candidates — including Johnson — who earn enough support to move on to a runoff election. The city’s powerful Chicago Teachers Union backed Johnson in the last cycle and its political action committee spent several million dollars on the race.

Johnson will face Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, State Comptroller Susana Mendoza, US Representative Mike Quigley and former Chicago Housing Authority Chief Executive Officer Matt Brewer among a field of at least half a dozen candidates.

A longtime friend of former President Barack Obama, Giannoulias is expected to be a top contender and has already assembled a $22 million war chest, aided by support from business and political leaders.

items.title: US Energy Chief Downplays Chance of Hormuz Advance With Iran
body: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright cautioned oil traders against expecting a breakthrough on the Strait of Hormuz as Iran plans to pitch other Gulf countries on a deal for passage through the energy chokepoint.

“Counting on a consensual agreement with Iran today is certainly not a good bet,” Wright said in an interview on Sunday. He said markets will need to continue relying on transit that he said over the past seven days has supplied an average of 10 million barrels per day of crude and oil products through the Strait of Hormuz.

The Trump administration estimates an additional 4 to 5 million barrels per day has been carried away through pipelines. While attacks late last week led to the closing of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, the US expects it to be back online soon, according to an administration official who asked not to be named to speak candidly about the matter.
That means “we’re back to two-thirds or north of two-thirds of the previous flows,” Wright said. “So the world oil markets are tighter than we’d like today, but they’re not overly tight.”

Iran plans to unveil an agreement on a temporary shipping lane through the strait on Monday in Oman after an unusual round of regional diplomacy over the waterway that included rare direct talks between Iran and Abu Dhabi.

Wright spoke in Vienna, where he plans to deliver a stern warning to Iran at the International Atomic Energy Agency. The United Nations nuclear watchdog’s annual general conference begins Monday, and the Trump administration’s top energy official said Tehran’s nuclear program will end “one way or another.”

“We prefer to negotiate,” Wright told Bloomberg News. “Or, they can continue to have a covert, buried, lied-about, hidden nuclear weapons program and face the US military, which will assure they do not develop nuclear weapons.”
Read More: Hormuz Meeting With Iran and Gulf Nations Delayed, Oman Says

Last week, the US led an IAEA motion that referred Iran back to the UN Security Council. The Islamic Republic hasn’t allowed international inspectors to verify the state and location of its stockpile of near-bomb grade uranium since June 2025, when Israel and the US attacked its sprawling nuclear program.
“To have no inspectors on the ground, no visibility, that’s another level of noncompliance and absolutely it’s concerning,” Wright said.

IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi last week echoed comments by US President Donald Trump that new activity had been detected at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site suspected of housing nuclear-related activities.

“There are some indications that there is movement around this construction site,” Grossi said in a Sept. 10 interview. “We don’t have any concrete information as to activities that may be taking place there.”

The US and Israel want Iran to dismantle its centrifuge program and cease enriching uranium. Centrifuges are the fast-spinning machines separating uranium isotopes and are a critical technology in the making of nuclear fuel for power or weapons.
“We can supply fuel from outside the country,” Wright said. “They could join the community of nations again and bring peace and prosperity to their people.”

The US is close to bolstering its own uranium supply chain, according to Wright. The Department of Energy is closing in on “long-term uranium production and partnership” deals, he said without providing details.
The US nuclear industry remains heavily dependent on imports of uranium products to fuel the reactors that generate about a fifth of the nation’s electricity.

items.title: Amodei Essay: Anthropic AI Apocalypse Warning Is Far Too Weak
body: Days after one of his former employees made public warnings about artificial intelligence’s threat to humanity, Anthropic’s boss Dario Amodei has responded with what looks like a solution. He’s published an essay proposing that AI labs should slow down their most cutting-edge research, to address signs that the technology might spin out of control.

On the face of it this sounds reasonable. Anthropic frames itself as the most safety-conscious AI company, and Amodei has talked about leading a “race to the top” in setting standards of vigilance for others to follow when building powerful systems. But this was probably an impossible ideal from the start.

The more powerful AI agents become, the more likely they are to deceive humans and the harder they can be to monitor. This makes the mission of Amodei, and fellow pioneers such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to create superintelligent systems look increasingly difficult to reconcile with any safety ethos. The dangers of trying to design such models may simply be too great.

Amodei said in television interviews on Sunday that he agreed with the views of his former employee Jacob Coxon, who wrote on X that the people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Unsurprisingly, Amodei noted Coxon’s point that Anthropic was the safest pair of hands to construct the technology.

The Anthropic boss’s 3,831-word essay is vague on what to do about it, though, calling airily for coordination between governments and industry. His most concrete recommendation is that external auditors should embed with his company and its rivals to check they’re following proper safety practices.Amodei explicitly says “pacing” does not mean halting model training or technical progress.

Yet this simply kicks the can down the road. If Amodei truly agreed with Coxon, he would halt his firm’s most cutting-edge research, particularly anything to do with building AI agents that can create their own successors independently. Coxon warned specifically about this technique, known as recursive self improvement (or RSI).

Researchers working on RSI argue that it can be developed in a “sandboxed” environment to stop it doing harm on the wider internet. But AI models — which can now carry out tasks on the internet that go way beyond the generation of content — have escaped before. OpenAI’s agents did exactly that before hacking a fellow AI firm Hugging Face recently. The evidence of the past few months shows AIs can deceive their human overseers, manipulate people into helping them and exploit security vulnerabilities to achieve a goal.

Completely stopping that research sounds extreme, but there is a precedent for scientists deciding that some work is simply too dangerous to continue without stronger safeguards. In 1974, leading biologists called a voluntary moratorium on certain gene-splicing experiments because of fears about their potential hazards.The pause lasted until the 1975 Asilomar conference established strict conditions under which research could resume. And some nations such as the United Arab Emirates have agreed to forgo uranium enrichment because of the proliferation risks.

For the investors who’ve plowed fortunes into Anthropic and fellow pioneering labs — and into the vast infrastructure needed to support their computational needs — calling a halt might appear to blow a hole in the prospects of Amodei and others joining the public markets. Indeed, OpenAI’s Altman agreed with his rival on the need to slow things down, and used the moment to say his firm wouldn’t be doing an initial public offering this year.

But it’s worth remembering that many enterprises would rather use smaller, cheaper AI models for specific tasks, not expensive frontier tools like superintelligence. OpenAI, for instance, cut the price of its smaller Luna model by 80% in July as corporate customers scrutinized their spending on the technology. The most obvious commercial opportunity for AI companies right now is the enterprise market. And it’s blocked in large part because businesses can’t figure out how to plug the basic technology into their workflows.

Much of the hundreds of billions of dollars of value still to be unlocked from AI would come simply from implementing the tech that was built in the last two years. Anthropic could still be an extremely valuable company if it focused primarily on helping businesses and consumers integrate its existing models into their work and lives, taking on the more boring role of IT provider rather than a laboratory racing to superintelligence.

Whether from naivety or hubris, Amodei still wants it both ways. He believes his company can safely build and control AI systems even as they are becoming difficult to steer. And yet, in the past year both Anthropic and OpenAI have for competitive reasons obscured details about how their models process information, making them more difficult to monitor. Amodei’s own essay acknowledges the problem, saying that researchers still understand only “a tiny fraction” of what happens inside their models.

He writes that within 6-12 months, the kind of swarm that attacked Hugging Face “could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” and this “worries” him. Notwithstanding his tendency to exaggerate (remember his white-collar bloodbath?) that is an alarming prospect. And it underscores the strange contradiction he won’t let go of, rooted in a belief common in Silicon Valley, that the chance of an AI utopia outweighs the risks, and that superintelligence is inevitable and so the “good guys” must get there first.

But inevitability is a mightily poor argument for continuing research you believe could destroy civilization. Amodei’s unstoppable determination to create superintelligence needs to go on the back burner and his “slowdown” should be a full stop.

items.title: Trump Defends His Support for Irish Unity Despite UK Uproar
body: President Donald Trump defended his remarks calling for the unification of Ireland as “fairly routine,” standing by comments that have sparked a controversy in Northern Ireland.

“I’ve always loved the people of Ireland, and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland, and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together,” Trump told reporters Sunday as he attended the Irish Open in Doonbeg.
“So that’s only my opinion. And by the way, many people agree,” he said. “I made what I consider to be a fairly routine comment. I’ve had so much support on that.”
Trump’s comments Sunday came in response to a question about whether UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should hold a referendum on a united Ireland, though the US president sidestepped that matter.
A day earlier, during a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would like to see Ireland unified.
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified. I have friends on both sides,” Trump said at that time, adding that he thought it would happen eventually.

Martin said some of the response to Trump’s comments “is an overreaction.” “I think if everyone keeps a calm perspective on things you know, we will take it from there. I’m meeting the British Prime Minister next week,” Martin told reporters Sunday.
Martin said he believes in Irish unity but refused to be drawn on any possible timeline. “What I don’t want to do is to go back to the failed sort of approaches historically.”

Trump’s remarks put him at odds with Burnham and other British leaders and have led critics to question whether the US was changing what has been a mostly neutral position on the constitutional future of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, a region of the UK.
The US played a major role in the brokering of the Good Friday Agreement, the landmark treaty that brought an end to decades of violence in Northern Ireland known as the Troubles.
Earlier: Trump Says He’d Love to See a ‘United’ Ireland During Visit

A spokesperson for Burnham’s office said Saturday that the PM’s position on a border poll, as a vote on unification is known, remains unchanged after Trump’s remarks and that he was “committed to upholding the Good Friday Agreement.” Burnham said last month that a referendum on a united Ireland was “off the table.”

A vote can only be called by the UK’s Secretary of State for Northern Ireland when it “appears likely” that a majority of people in the region would support reunification, as stipulated in the Good Friday Agreement.
“Everybody says that and then things happen,” Trump told a reporter Sunday.
The backlash to Trump’s comments crossed party lines in the UK, with a populist ally — Reform UK’s leader Nigel Farage — also criticizing his statement.

“Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom. The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification. I disagree with President Trump,” Farage said in a post on X.

Former Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams, who was the party’s chief when the Good Friday Agreement was reached in 1998, said Trump’s remarks only reflected “broad North American sentiment” and said he welcomed the president’s remarks even though they disagreed on many other issues.

items.title: Trump Demands Ukraine Halt Refinery Strikes as Diesel Surges
body: President Donald Trump said he’d warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting oil refineries in Russia amid strikes that have shut down diesel refining and helped drive prices for the fuel to record levels.

“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said Sunday on the sidelines of the Amgen Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland. “Let him go after targets — but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel.”

Trump’s demand threatens to deprive Ukraine of one of its most powerful tools in damaging Russia’s economy in response to the war that President Vladimir Putin started. Russia has intensified missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, including targeting power and energy infrastructure. Kyiv has hit back with strikes on oil refineries that have led to widespread fuel shortages in many Russian regions.
Read more: Ukraine Strikes Russian Refineries as Odesa Ports Targeted

Beyond its impact on Russia’s economy, the gasoline deficit is making the war that’s now in its fifth year more visible to ordinary Russians as drivers across much of the country confront limits on fuel availability.
Read More: Ukraine’s Record Strikes Push Russians Back to Gasoline Lines

Diesel and gasoline are produced at the same refineries and Ukrainian strikes have disrupted output of both fuels. The impact on diesel production pushed Moscow to ban exports, but it’s gasoline shortages that are being felt more directly across Russia.
Russia’s diesel export restrictions due to Ukrainian strikes have added pressure to a global market already squeezed by the war in the Middle East.

The Kremlin welcomes Trump’s call for Ukraine to refrain from strikes on Russian oil refineries, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday, according to Interfax. Peskov didn’t say whether Russia would be ready to stop attacking Ukrainian energy facilities in response, the news agency said.

Russia’s diesel-export restrictions have kept enough fuel away from the international oil market to affect global supplies, Peskov said. Before Kyiv’s flurry of attacks on Russia’s refining industry, the country was a major exporter of diesel, accounting for about 10% of worldwide trade.
Average diesel prices rose above $6 per gallon in the US for the first time ever last week, driven by supply shortages caused by the war in Iran as well as the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The potential economic ramifications are enormous. While most American motorists focus closely on the cost of unleaded gasoline, which has also risen 54% from a $2.795 low in January, diesel is an essential power source for long-haul trucks, freight trains and farm equipment.
Related: California Gas Station With $9.99 Diesel Exemplifies Fuel Crisis

For Trump, the issue poses a particular political peril ahead of the November midterm elections that will determine control of the House and Senate. Increased fuel prices are already cutting revenue and forcing business owners to charge more for goods as energy-driven inflation flows downstream, adding to cost-of-living concerns that already weigh on the president’s Republican Party in the November contests.
Trump on Sunday emphasized the global concern on fuel prices as he described his warning to Zelenskyy to steer clear of refining facilities in Russia.

“We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets,” Trump said. “Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting the world. We don’t want him to hit diesel fuel. He’s hitting diesel refineries.”
It wasn’t immediately clear how Kyiv would respond to Trump’s admonition or when the conversation he described took place.

The Trump administration has already warned Ukraine to curtail strikes on other energy infrastructure in the region, particularly Caspian Pipeline Consortium facilities and non-Russian vessels in the Black Sea.

Russia Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov last week rejected a moratorium on attacks against ships carrying civilian goods in the Black Sea, saying it was impossible to monitor and unacceptable to Moscow, the Interfax news service reported.

Trump has sought to allay concerns about energy prices, and on Sunday reiterated his view that costs will plummet after the Iran war is over. He predicted that conflict would end “right after” or “maybe before” the midterms.

items.title: Trump Says He's Not Worried About Xi Calling Off Summit
body: President Donald Trump said he is not worried that Chinese President Xi Jinping will cancel a highly anticipated visit later this month.

“No, I’m not worried about that,” Trump told reporters as he attended the Irish Open in Doonbeg on Sunday. “We have a great relationship. He wants to get along, and we want it. We’re going to get along.”
Trump’s comments follow a recent report that China had warned the US that it would scrap Xi’s upcoming visit if the US approved new arms sales to Taiwan, a major point of contention for Beijing.

Trump has said he is weighing a $14 billion arms deal with Taiwan, the self-governing democratic island, that China sees as part of its country. Xi has warned the US president in the past that there is a potential for conflict if the issue of Taiwan is mismanaged.
Trump has previously said he talked to Xi “a lot” about Taiwan during their summit in May, and said in an interview at the time with Fox News that he wanted Beijing to “cool down” about the issue.

The leaders of the world’s two largest economies are slated to meet face-to-face  later this month in Washington, as they seek to manage tensions over Taiwan as well as trade, artificial intelligence and the Middle East. While the May summit was marked by displays of warmth between the two leaders, there have been fresh strains between the countries, in particular over the Iran war.

China is the main buyer of Iranian oil and Beijing has resisted Trump’s calls to cut off economic ties with Tehran. The US president has sought to ramp up economic pressure on the Islamic Republic in a bid to force it to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the critical energy waterway largely shuttered since the war’s launch, and to strike a deal to end the conflict.

Xi, for his part, has appeared in no rush to help Trump end a war the US launched alongside Israel and which is now in its seventh month. Taking stronger action against Chinese firms that support Iran’s economy would also risk bigger blowback for the US.

Both nations appear eager to keep relations on track following a tit-for-tat tariff war last year that unnerved financial markets and raised worries about a global economic downturn. A subsequent trade truce has largely held despite persistent tensions over export controls for rare earth minerals and cutting-edge technologies. That truce, though, is set to expire Nov. 10.

items.title: Apple's iPhone Duo Will Make Foldable Phones the New Normal; Apple Store Revamp
body: Apple’s iPhone Duo will go down as one of the company’s historic products, eventually turning foldable phones into the new normal. Also: The company is preparing a big retail shake-up, and its upcoming game controller will likely come from Beats.
Last week in Power On: Tim Cook’s CEO-like pay package   shows he isn’t going anywhere.

Apple Inc.’s Tim Cook is clearly a company man. The longtime executive, who ushered in the first major new product of his CEO tenure with the industry-changing Apple Watch in 2015, could have seized the glory of introducing the company’s inaugural foldable phone. Instead, he put Apple first and let his successor take the spotlight with last week’s launch of the iPhone Duo.

Yes, Cook is getting paid an   unorthodox $47 million next year to remain at Apple as executive chairman. But I believe the Duo is so impressive — and such a significant reinvention of the iPhone — that Cook could have easily chosen to make it his final product introduction, rather than   the first for new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus.

The move means the last major new device of Cook’s tenure was the Vision Pro headset — by   all accounts a sales flop because of its price and size, despite being technologically remarkable. Unlike that device, the iPhone Duo is likely to one day be mentioned as just a notch below the 1998 iMac, 2001 iPod, 2010 iPad and 2015 Apple Watch. It simply has that kind of game-changing potential.

For years, Apple watchers have been clamoring for something entirely new. Whether that was augmented reality glasses, a lightweight mixed-reality headset or some other new wearable infused with artificial intelligence, some device was expected to finally succeed the traditional iPhone. It turns out Apple had   another idea in mind: an evolution of the iPhone itself.

To me, the iPhone Duo elicits the same feeling I had with the original iPhone or iPad during the Steve Jobs era. It feels fresh, has an impressive fit and finish, and makes clear that this is a device with the potential to change the computing landscape for years. Though the Duo   isn’t a new concept, its software adaptations, high-quality materials and durability put it in a   different league than previous foldables.

While it’s still true that Apple needs to produce new AI wearables and other peripherals, those kinds of products will always exist around a central computing device. For decades, that was the Mac. Then it became the iPhone. In any case, the hub needs to be something powerful with a screen. Even as wearables become more prevalent, people are still going to want something they can carry with them that has a display for reading, gaming and videoconferencing.

AI devices are getting close to being able to handle text messaging, calendars, research, emails, phone calls and other tasks on a user’s behalf. But there’s no universe in which a gadget with a tiny screen — or no screen at all — takes over all of the other things people use their phones for. That’s why the smartphone is going nowhere. In fact, it’s only getting more powerful and capable.

The other factor here is that Apple seems to have figured out the use cases for the iPhone Duo — in other words, why people should buy one. Apple pulled off something similar with the original iPhone: The company initially sold it as a mobile internet machine before improving on the pitch a year later by turning the device into an app platform with seemingly limitless potential. The iPad’s selling points were less obvious at launch, but it quickly found its place as a multipurpose device that people use for a wide range of tasks.

Apple stumbled out of the gate with the Watch, branding it largely as a fashion accessory and timepiece before saving the product by repositioning it around health and fitness. And then there was the Vision Pro, which was a real disaster when it came to compelling uses. One of   the better ideas involved doctors using the device during surgery — hardly the kind of task that is going to move millions of units.

With the iPhone Duo, I think Apple has gotten it right from day one. The company has gone all-in on video watching, gaming and photography, while adding features that take advantage of the foldable design. There’s an upgraded StandBy mode for widgets, new camera and FaceTime capabilities that use the second display as a viewfinder or monitor for another person, and an alarm-clock mode that capitalizes on the device being able to prop itself up.

And this is all part of a broader arc for the iPhone. When the product launched, it upended the telecom industry. Consumers quickly began abandoning dumb phones and flip-style devices for smartphones. Not everyone went out and bought an iPhone, of course, but the shift toward touch-screen slab phones with more advanced operating systems happened rapidly. Even if the iPhone wasn’t the first smartphone, it was the product that helped kick off the market shift.

Just before the iPhone arrived, smartphones accounted for only about 6% of global mobile-phone shipments. Six years after the iPhone’s launch, smartphones became the majority of phones sold worldwide. Today, they account for about 85% of handsets sold globally, even if Apple holds only around a fifth of the market on its own.

Foldables remain at a much earlier stage. Though the category entered the mainstream market seven years ago with Samsung Electronics Co.’s Galaxy Fold, such devices represent only about 2% of global smartphone shipments today. Thanks to the iPhone Duo, I think that number is going to rise rapidly — both from sales of Apple’s device and competing phones that embrace some of the same design elements.

My prediction is that, within a decade, foldables will make up the majority of new phone sales. Users will increasingly see the benefits of having a larger display in their pocket and a device that can replace a laptop or tablet for many tasks. Foldables could become the do-it-all computing products of the future.

That said, this transition won’t happen as quickly as the original smartphone shift. The reason for that is simple: Foldable phones are very expensive and require compromises. At $1,999 and up, the Duo costs more than two standard iPhones combined. The amount is even higher in some overseas markets, where   Apple is charging more to help keep the US starting price below $2,000.

But the technology will gradually become more affordable — and not just because of what happens to the price. Today, the   Apple Upgrade leasing program is only available in the US. At some point, it will go international, and Apple will put the monthly leasing rate at the center of its marketing — rather than the phone’s full purchase price. Technology costs will come down over time as well. In 2017, the price of admission for an iPhone with Face ID and an OLED screen was $999. These days, you can get a similarly equipped iPhone 17e for $699, even after its recent price increase.

Eventually, Apple will have more than a singular iPhone Duo. It will have a family of foldable iPhones, just as Samsung has expanded its lineup into multiple variations. The Duo brand itself should help accommodate this. Apple may have chosen the name because it wanted something with three letters — matching Air and Pro — that reflected the device’s dual-screen nature. But the moniker also leaves room for a suffix.

It’s easy to foresee Apple launching an iPhone Duo Max with a larger display, or perhaps an iPhone Duo SE or iPhone Duo mini as either a stripped-down version or clamshell model. Though many people within Apple thought the company would go with the iPhone Ultra name, that wouldn’t have been as versatile. An iPhone Ultra Max or iPhone Ultra SE just wouldn’t make much sense.

By early next year, I expect the iPhone Duo to become the predominant foldable phone on the market. Demand will be so intense that people will scalp the device for sale overseas, eBay prices will soar, and supply shortages will reach extreme levels — potentially even eclipsing the Mac shortages Apple has faced this year because of the AI boom.

But Apple won’t remain the dominant player forever. The iPhone Duo will follow the trajectory of the original iPhone. That means its impact will be turning foldables into the main form of mobile computing and pushing the rest of the industry to dramatically increase its investment in the category. In other words, the iPhone Duo is so impressive that it will turn foldables into the new normal.

In case you missed it, I answered dozens of questions about Apple’s product launch and the future of the company under new CEO John Ternus in a Live Q&A with Bloomberg Businessweek Daily co-host Tim Stenovec. I encourage you   to      listen to the Live Q&A here  .

Apple prepares a retail store shake-up with a renewed focus on a dedicated Genius Bar and revamped pickup and classes areas. It’s no secret that Apple has   changed its retail strategy over the past half-decade. Rather than continuing the rapid expansion of its stores, the company has opened new locations more selectively. It also has focused on upgrading, relocating and — in some cases — closing older stores around the world. I’m told Apple plans to accelerate this renovation spree in coming years, making some major design changes along the way.
Here’s what Apple has planned:

A fraction of these changes have already appeared in a handful of Apple stores, but the plan now is to bring the full refreshed look to most upgraded and newly opened locations over time. Apple has spent the past year testing the concepts internationally, and the company plans a broader global rollout over the next several years.

Apple is also enforcing stricter rules for employees during morning meetings before stores open. Staff is expected to remain standing, refrain from drinking beverages or using devices, and stay fully engaged. When stores open — five minutes before the advertised time — the entire team, regardless of role, is expected to applaud as the first customers enter.

Leaked Apple-made game controllers are for the iPhone and will likely be sold under the Beats brand. A bit over a week ago,  code inside the iOS operating system revealed that Apple has two game controllers under development. Here’s what I know: The company has indeed been working on gaming controllers for the iPhone for a bit over a year, with the goal of competing with a slew of popular third-party options. Apple sees this as a growing market and wants in.

But here’s the interesting part: I’ve consistently heard that the controllers are destined to launch under Apple’s Beats brand and that product engineering and conception are being led by Beats executives. The company has increasingly been using Beats as a way to experiment with new product categories and capitalize on the third-party accessories market without putting certain types of products under the more premium Apple brand.

For example, Beats now sells a range of iPhone cases and USB-C cables that don’t necessarily fit Apple’s usual approach to design. A controller makes sense in that context. To reach a broad audience, it has to be relatively affordable, which means avoiding some of the more expensive materials and finishes typically associated with Apple products. The culture and lifestyle around gaming controllers also could fit naturally under the Beats umbrella.

Q: Where’s the new Apple TV?A: I’ve been reporting for a while that the company is preparing to upgrade its set-top box, and it’s been a frustratingly long wait. In the four years since the last Apple TV box was released, the device has become sluggish — with outdated audio and smart-home technology — and it isn’t as cool or cheap as the competition. The situation only got worse after the memory-chip shortage sent the starting price to $199 from $129. But none of that changes the reality: Though Apple has been trying to introduce a fresh set-top box since 2024, it wants the device to leverage the new Siri assistant. And what has been delayed since 2024? The new Siri. So Apple shelved the box until its Siri AI features were ready. The good news is, we’ve finally reached that point. I   expect the updated Apple TV this fall with Siri AI support and a faster chip. Enjoy.

Q: Do you think the iPhone Duo will eventually get Face ID and a telephoto camera?A: I’d bet that Face ID and a telephoto camera are the top two priorities on Apple’s list for future iPhone Duo models. Both are difficult to squeeze into such a thin device because the necessary components require significant depth — it’s fundamentally a physics problem. My guess is that Apple will solve both omissions by the third generation, but not purely by overcoming those physical constraints. It’ll probably be a combination of further component miniaturization and advances in artificial intelligence, allowing Apple to use smaller, less sophisticated depth-sensing and camera hardware while making up some of the difference computationally. We will get an early glimpse of that approach with the facial-recognition technology in Apple’s   upcoming smart-home hub.

items.title: Traders Hedging Stock Rally Split on Plunge or Drift Protection
body: Investors looking to hedge as the equity rally stalls in the face of rising interest rates and oil prices are split between protecting against a fast selloff or a slow grind lower.

A couple of factors have been working against stock-market hedgers lately. The S&P 500 Index has been mostly range-bound since the end of May, and for several periods this year realized moves have been larger during rallies than declines, which led to a phenomenon referred to as “spot-up/vol-up” in market parlance.

The smaller swings — especially lower — have made some traders more reluctant to pay up for outright short-dated put options protection, given the risk that premiums decay without a sufficiently large downside move. So while some investors are buying calls on the Cboe Volatility Index or S&P 500 puts, others are becoming more creative in how they position for a decline.
Read more: Stocks Are Grinding Lower and Gapping Higher Under Trump

“With the reversal of ‘spot up/vol up,’ we’ve seen some trades playing ‘spot down/vol down’ — such as dual binary options playing SPX down, VIX down to play the grind lower,” said Antoine Porcheret, head of institutional structuring for the UK, Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Citigroup Inc.

A “grind lower” has been a popular phrase and trade in the last few years as several investors viewed a moderate selloff, rather than a sudden plunge, as a worthwhile scenario to hedge and speculate on.

These dual binary trades playing equities down amid lower volatility reflect the broader lack of shock and surprise that now characterizes both the AI theme and geopolitical risk, which makes the case for owning volatility less obvious. Even with the VIX sitting around 15.5, below its four-year average, it’s still near the top of the the range relative to actual market swings.
Read more: Wall Street Touts ‘Grind Lower’ Trades as Iran Weighs on Stocks
Events such as US non-farm payrolls were once consistently big market movers, but without a shocking result markets can now settle very quickly.

Yet even though economic headline risks have somewhat faded, equities still appear highly sensitive to rates. So all eyes will be on this week’s Federal Reserve rate decision, with market sentiment leaning toward the US central bank raising rates.

With long-term US bond yields rising to multiyear highs, stagflation-style option payoffs playing equities down, rates up have attracted flows earlier this year. JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategists recently pitched dual binary options to leverage this scenario into year-end.
Read more: Leverage That Fueled US Stock Rally Becomes a Growing Concern

To be sure, there are still signs of investors placing bets with a more convex payoff, wagering that volatility is likely to jump with the equity rally facing multiple perils. Besides rising interest rates, those include high oil prices as the US-Iran war rages on, and support for a stronger yen — which threatens an unwind of the carry trade, similar to what happened when stocks plunged and volatility spiked in August 2024.

That has prompted some investors to opt for hedging via long outright VIX calls, with the general bid for vol of vol convexity visible via the index’s call skew. More than 275,000 lots of October and November VIX calls were bought in large blocks in the past couple of weeks.

“The biggest theme within the flow has been in hedging activity,” said Porcheret. “The outright long volatility plays have been more cautious, for example long knock-in forward start variance, where you only own volatility if the market rallies.”
And while some leveraged bets stay pricey, there are still investors ready to take the other side of the trade, seeking to collect premium.

“We are effectively seeing demand at both ends of the spectrum: greater interest in systematic protection and convexity, while investors continue to allocate to short volatility strategies for carry and yield enhancement,” said Adrien Geliot, chief executive officer of Premialab. “The key distinction is increasingly around portfolio objective and implementation rather than a broad shift from short to long volatility.”

items.title: Trump Downplays AI Concerns as CEOs Call for Slowing Pace
body: President Donald Trump downplayed the growing alarm over risks from artificial intelligence after some of the industry’s leaders called for slowing the pace of development of the technology.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump said Sunday to reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open. “And we can put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up.”

Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei issued a lengthy blog post Saturday calling on the industry to slow down and saying that the effort requires industry and global coordination. OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who runs xAI Corp., swiftly endorsed Amodei’s message.
In particular, Amodei said his company would implement new safety steps including the use of third-party evaluators, an idea that Altman also said he’ll follow.

But there are questions about how committed the AI leaders will be about moderating the pace of development of their most advanced — and most lucrative — models, particularly given the intense competition from Chinese rivals.
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Sunday that Amodei’s proposal for additional AI safeguards could serve as a model for the private sector, including by giving independent observers access to the models.

Speaking on Fox News Sunday, Hassett called AI safety a “solvable problem.” He said AI is advancing rapidly enough to potentially overcome existing cybersecurity defenses, but companies are also developing new safeguards.
Read More: What Happens If the AI Boom Never Pays Off?

“If you look at the movement that the private sector is making, the fact that Elon and OpenAI folks have already supported the actually pretty sensible moves that Dario is advising, I think that that’s a good movement forward, a good step forward,” Hassett said, adding that Trump administration officials Sean Cairncross and Michael Kratsios are also studying the issue.

Some Democrats have seized on the risks around AI as a big issue heading into the November midterms and the 2028 presidential election. Former President Barack Obama told an audience at a private fundraiser last week that Democrats should make AI oversight a central issue in their campaigns, according to the New York Times.

Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat from Delaware who has helped introduce a bill to protect AI whistleblowers, said a lack of expertise in Congress risks hampering AI regulation as the Trump administration maintains a hands-off approach.

“That’s one of our real challenges: that we’ve got folks in the Senate and the House who are not as engaged, as curious, as current on this rapidly evolving technology as we need,” Coons said on Bloomberg This Weekend. “We need agreement from Republicans and Democrats in Congress to put aside our partisan pre-election bickering and put in place some real guardrails before AI goes off the rails.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC’s This Week that House Democrats will meet as a caucus on Tuesday morning to discuss possible action on AI.

Speaker Mike Johnson called for a partnership between the tech industry and government to find AI guardrails, saying his message to the companies is that they “have a corporate responsibility to make sure your products are safe.”

“We have got to summon everybody together,” the Louisiana Republican said on CNN’s State of the Union. “I have talked to the president about this as well. They probably should be summoned together at the White House.”

Amodei said he thinks there is a role for government regulation when it comes to AI. “Regulation allows the public and its elected representatives to have a say, and limits what the private companies can do,” the Anthropic chief said in an interview that aired Sunday on CBS’s Sunday Morning.
But David Sacks, Trump’s former AI czar who now co-chairs his technology advisory council, said that AI companies don’t need government permission to slow down or be more responsible.

“You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack,” he wrote in a post on X. “The market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorized ways.”
At the same time, it’s unclear whether Chinese companies or the government in Beijing will be interested in working with US firms on a slowdown or guardrails.

Speaking on CBS, Amodei said a longer-term agreement with China would make sense to put a “speed limit on the rate of AI progress,” but he acknowledged it may be unrealistic. Verification would need to be “ironclad,” he said, because of the military advantages of pulling ahead. “Honestly, I don’t know if it’s possible. But we should try.”

The surge in safety concerns surrounding AI coincides with a growing backlash against the technology in the US, fueled in part by objections to the strain on local resources imposed by new data centers needed to support the technology. Concerns that AI is driving up electricity bills and potentially taking away jobs have made it a central issue in the midterms.
Read more: Anthropic’s AI Warning May Weigh on Chips, But Trade Seen Intact

Another factor weighing on the market is whether the vast sums being poured into AI and related infrastructure will pay off. The scrutiny has left high-valuation shares linked to the technology particularly vulnerable, with signs of increased spending or weaker returns triggering selloffs in stocks.
“They’re bringing up things that won’t happen, but whoever wins, with AI, wins,” Trump said.

items.title: Trump Pushes Fed to Lower Rates Despite Pressure For a Hike
body: President Donald Trump reiterated that the US should have the lowest interest rates in the world even as his handpicked chair for the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, faces renewed pressure to raise borrowing costs.

“We should be paying — the United States is so strong — we should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world, regardless of their formulas,” Trump told reporters Sunday in Ireland, where he is attending the Irish Open.
Asked if he expected the central bank to raise rates at its meeting next week, Trump said: “I don’t know.”

Trump’s comments follow data released Friday showing US consumer prices rose more than expected in August. The Fed is likely to view those numbers as pushing it toward the first rate increase in three years. The inflation data led traders to boost expectations for a Fed hike, with an 86% chance of a move in September and two increases priced in by the end of the year.
Earlier: Warsh Faces Intensifying Pressure to Raise Rates After Hot CPI
The US economy faces higher energy prices with the US war on Iran now in its seventh month, and Trump’s tariff policies have also complicated the picture for the Fed’s inflation target.

Trump repeatedly assailed former Fed chief Jerome Powell for his unwillingness to lower borrowing costs more aggressively. While Warsh hasn’t faced the same pressure after taking over the central bank’s top post, Trump in recent weeks has signaled continuing frustration with the Fed’s policy stance.

Even as Trump has vented his frustration with the Fed, he’s suggested that Warsh’s hands may be tied by what the president has called a “very political” board of governors. Earlier in September, Trump also floated cutting off trade with certain economies that the US has a trade deficit with if the central bank did not lower borrowing costs, but it was unclear how the threat would help ease rates.
“I know more about formulas than anybody, and with the best credit in the world, we make other countries rich. We could turn that off in two minutes,” Trump said Sunday.
Later, when asked by reporters if he would actually follow through with that threat, Trump said: “Yeah, I’m going to do that with some nations.”
“It will take place over a period of time,” he said.

Voters have given Trump poor marks on both the war and his handling of the economy. Concerns over higher costs of living that touch on energy, housing, healthcare and groceries are a top issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections that threaten to break Republicans’ control of Congress.
