items.title: LA's Lucas Museum Shines Spotlight on Architect Ma Yansong
body: Hello and welcome to Bloomberg’s weekly design digest. I’m Kriston Capps, staff writer and editor for Bloomberg CityLab and your guide to the world of architecture and the people who build things.
This week the US commemorated the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks in New York. Sign up to keep up: Subscribe to get the Design Edition newsletter every Sunday.

After years of development, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is finally opening its doors. On Sept. 22, fans of Star Wars, pulp fiction, Frank Frazetta, comic strips, Vampirella, graphic illustration, Norman Rockwell and much more will get the chance to indulge in George Lucas’s peerless collection of popular art. Expect to see selfies with the museum’s bronze statue of Princess Leia strangling Jabba the Hutt for the rest of your life.

While the fanboys will no doubt line up outside the museum’s grand arching entrance, critics so far are less enthralled. As Carolina A. Miranda writes, the problem with the museum isn’t the collection. It’s Lucas’s philosophy that good art doesn’t need any explanation. The museum’s installations of graphic art are presented without context, subtext or even wall text.
The building itself, meanwhile, has its own story to tell.

The Lucas building is the work of Ma Yansong, founder of the Beijing architecture practice MAD. The museum is not his first big project in the US — the firm also designed One River North, a multifamily building in Denver that looks like it has a giant crack in it — but it’s nevertheless making quite a splash.

Yet it’s not exactly unique: The curvilinear, biomorphic design of the Lucas Museum building is similar to many of Ma’s projects scattered across China. The building even resembles earlier iterations for the museum when it was planned for Chicago and San Francisco. Miranda writes that the building doesn’t draw upon its environs in Exposition Park: The garage and loading dock for the Lucas, for example, face the entrance of the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. Los Angeles residents might have expected more synergy there.

In a sense Ma’s design is the perfect illustration of Lucas’s project: a building shaped like a spaceship, plopped down in LA, boom, no context necessary. After years of architectural projects driven by sensitivity to their regions or surroundings, maybe the Lucas marks a vibe shift — the return of the starchitect.

Architect Sanjay Puri describes a delightfully eclectic set of influences that led him to become a designer: the postwar modernism of Rotterdam, the Brutalist architecture of Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh and Ayn Rand’s The Fountainhead. None of those inputs exactly explains his Escher-like plan for Prestige University in Indore, Madhya Pradesh. Bloomberg’s Meneka Dashi spoke with Puri and the designers behind two other contemporary projects — the Malabar Group headquarters in Kozhikode, Kerala, by Tony Joseph and Terminal 2 of Guwahati’s Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport by Nuru Karim — to find the pulse of contemporary architecture projects in India.

In the weeks and months following 9/11, as authorities cleaned the wreckage at Ground Zero, they amassed thousands of pieces of steel debris. In advance of the 10th anniversary of the attacks, the Port Authority designed a program to distribute these pieces from the buildings. Fragments of the Twin Towers made their way across the nation and indeed the world. Bloomberg CityLab’s Marie Patino talked to sociologist Max Holleran and artist and writer Samuel Holleran, who tracked the trajectory of these fragments — and the many local memorials in which they were incorporated — in a new book, Scattered Steel.

The most unique remembrance about 9/11 that I read this week was Christopher Hawthorne’s lecture on Herbert Muschamp, architecture critic for The New York Times at the time of the attacks, and his failure to interrogate the rebuilding process: “It remains an open question whether a Times critic with a firmer grasp of the subjects central to the rebuilding effort—not just architecture but real-estate development, urban design, civic memory, and not least bare-knuckled municipal politics—might have used the paper’s bully pulpit to turn that effort in a more enlightened direction.” (Punch List)

Emily Hamilton and Yonah Freemark find a novel culprit behind the absurd school drop-off lines that plague parents: “Before 1950, the median American high school in our sample sat on a 17-acre site. The typical high school built since then sits on nearly 40 acres. Similar changes have occurred among elementary schools, too, in tandem with a well-documented collapse in the share of students who walk or bike to school. In some places, it’s led to parents and kids sitting in comically long drop-off and pickup lines that contribute to traffic congestion on nearby streets.” (The Argument)

David Freedlander profiles Andrew Berman, a neighborhood activist committed to keeping new construction out of New York’s West Village: “Berman’s project has been remarkably successful over the last quarter-century. By the start of 2002, when Berman started at Greenwich Village Society for Historic Preservation, there were only 86 historic districts in the city; 12 years later, there were 131.” (New York)

items.title: Fayed Abuse Victims Seek Up to £150 Million From Harrods
body: Almost 300 women who say they were sexually abused by former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed want as much as £150 million ($203 million) in compensation from the luxury department store, more than double the amount it’s set aside.

The £62 million provision Harrods made in 2024 for redress payments will fall well short of what’s required, according to KP Law, which represents about 275 people, most of whom are former employees. The figure is likely to be at least £100 million and may be as much as £150 million, KP lawyer Lucy Traynor said.

The estimate is based on analysis of individual cases, taking into account lost earnings and pensions, the cost of treatment and other losses, Traynor said. KP has gone through tax records and consulted employment experts who have analyzed salaries for specific roles over time.

The provision is “an estimate, not a cap, and we will continue with our approach of assessing each individual claim on its merits and offering settlement based on that assessment,” a Harrods spokesperson said in a statement. External legal advisers and auditors helped Harrods with its analysis.

“Harrods is committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered,” the spokesperson said. More than 260 survivors have engaged with its redress program, with 113 claims settled to date, they said. Work continues “at a pace dictated by survivors and their legal representatives towards redress through the route of their choice,” they added.

Fayed has been accused of rape, sexual assault and harassment by scores of people over decades. Victims say that for years Harrods didn’t do enough to address the matter. Harrods has since accepted “vicarious liability” — responsibility for Fayed’s actions while he was chairman.

The billionaire owned the London store from 1985 to 2010, when his family sold it to Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund. The Egyptian businessman died in 2023 aged 94. After years denying women’s accounts about his abuse, Harrods said in a statement in 2024 that it was “utterly appalled by the allegations” and was “determined to do the right thing.”
Read More: Fayed’s Victims Say Harrods Hasn’t Fully Reckoned With His Abuse

The retailer created its own compensation plan for Fayed’s victims in March last year, saying it thought the offer was attractive for victims as they would not have to pay additional legal fees. It closed to new claims in March. Harrods has said the £62 million provision is its estimate for payouts made either via its process or anyone using their own lawyers.
The department store’s latest accounts show that as of January it paid out £4 million to claimants.

Trevor Gilbert, an employment expert witness who specializes in assessing career and earnings loss, said that £1 million isn’t an unusually high sum for someone who was on a particular career path but was then unable to pursue it. “They do not have to have been a particularly high earner for losses to reach that level,” he said.

“In my experience, claimants will generally advance their case toward the higher end of the range and defendants toward the lower end,” Gilbert said. “The parties may then seek to reach an agreed figure through negotiation or at a settlement meeting.”

James Counsell, a barrister who specializes in abuse cases, said it can be hard for claimants to win significant sums because English courts have traditionally awarded very low amounts to people who have suffered sexual abuse.

Victims are pressing for swifter resolution of their cases. Harrods and Fayed’s estate are locked in a legal dispute, as the company seeks to install an independent administrator to replace family members.

Harrods has said it’s seeking contributions to help meet the redress costs and has told KP it won’t negotiate until the outcome of the legal case. That relates to people claiming against both Harrods and the estate who make up the majority of KP’s cases.
A hearing is scheduled for November. The judge could make a decision at the time or later.

The appointment of “new, independent executors is for the benefit of all survivors — not just those represented by a single law firm — and all those with a potential claim against the estate,” the Harrods spokesperson said. “Any suggestion to survivors by their legal representatives that Harrods is preventing survivors from accessing compensation is a misrepresentation of the facts, and harmful to survivors’ trust in this process,” they added.
Justin Michaelson, a partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan LLP representing Fayed’s estate, said the executors take the allegations seriously but cannot comment further for legal reasons.
The time it’s taking is “incredibly distressing” for the claimants, KP’s Traynor said.

Among those KP represents were fashion buyers, people selected for Harrods’ management training program and personal assistants, with a significant number in their first jobs and their careers ahead of them. For some claimants, the bill runs into the millions of pounds, according to KP. The law firm will take a cut of claimants’ compensation payments.

“Two years ago, the world finally saw the scale of what Mohamed Fayed had been allowed to do,” Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, victims who co-chair the Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group, said in a statement Monday. “Two years later, hundreds of survivors are still waiting for truth, accountability, justice and proper compensation.”

Harrods has spent that time “telling the world it stands with survivors,” said Keaton Stone, whose wife Sophia was attacked by Fayed in the late 1980s. “What women have actually seen is delay. Some of these women have already waited thirty or forty years. Some are now in their seventies.” Stone investigated the Harrods owner for years leading to a BBC documentary in 2024.
A key factor in Harrods’ legal battle with the estate is what due diligence was done as part of the 2010 acquisition.

The Qatar Investment Authority hasn’t commented on the Fayed scandal. The fund conducted due diligence with the assistance of several external advisers including UK law firms, but the process didn’t identify allegations of serious misconduct related to Harrods, Bloomberg reported earlier this year. The QIA didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The Metropolitan Police Service is investigating whether anyone can be criminally charged over Fayed’s actions. It has interviewed seven individuals under caution. It has also sent a file to the Crown Prosecution Service for advice about whether a man in his 80s could be charged.

Harrods has said it’s also investigating whether anyone internally knew about Fayed’s abuse but hasn’t committed to publishing the findings. An employee left the business in 2025 in relation to the investigation, Harrods said.

The £62 million provision caused Harrods to report a £34 million loss for the financial year ending February 2025. Last month, the company painted an improved picture, swinging to an £85 million profit for its most recent financial year.

items.title: Emerging Markets Can Weather Fed Risk After Oil Jump and War
body: Emerging markets have defied war, $100 oil and rising Treasury yields this year. And despite worries of a US interest-rate hike, investors see reasons for this year’s rally to keep going.

While the asset class has been jolted after a fresh jump in oil prices added to Friday’s hot US inflation print in bolstering the case for a Federal Reserve rate increase this week, many money managers remain confident. Their bull case rests on improved policy credibility in many emerging markets and booming corporate earnings. Above all, they see little risk of a significant dollar rebound, which historically has been the main source of pain for emerging markets.
“I don’t hear any alarm bells ringing for emerging markets,” said Benoit Anne, senior managing director at MFS Investment Management.

The prospect of Fed rate hike “is not that big a deal for EM,” he said, adding that unlike in past rate-hike cycles, the dollar is being held back by concerns over US policy credibility. “To me, that dampens any potential shock for EM,” he said. He’s bullish on South African, Colombian and Hungarian local debt.
Read More: SK Hynix Closes In on Amazon as AI Debt Binge Reorders Risk

The dollar’s performance in 2026 bears that out. While getting a boost Monday, from increased Fed rate-hike bets, it’s down about 0.7% so far this year even as Treasury yields rose to multiyear highs. Emerging stocks, meanwhile, have gained about 21% this year — almost twice the S&P 500’s advance — while a gauge of currencies is near record highs.

Carry trades are booming too. Investors who borrow cheaply overseas to buy higher-yielding assets have reaped returns of as much as 30% in the likes of the Colombian peso, Turkish lira and Brazilian real.

Bank strategists are urging clients to sit tight. At JPMorgan Chase & Co, Luis Oganes and Nora Szentivanyi reckon emerging markets can weather two or three Fed hikes, especially countries where interest rates remain high.
“The emphasis on carry has been a core position this year,” they wrote, naming the Mexican peso, Brazilian real, Turkish lira and Hungarian forint as top picks.

There are risks to that view, such as the ongoing Middle East conflict that has sent energy prices soaring. Oil importers such as India and Indonesia have intervened to support their currencies, while South Africa has seen a sharp widening in its current account deficit.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh’s push to scale back policy guidance is adding another layer of uncertainty, making it trickier to gauge the outlook.
“If we move into a regime where the market’s perception is that the Fed might actually hike a lot more, then it’s a problem for the EM FX,” said Citigroup Inc. strategist Luis Costa.

Still, investors see emerging markets are better equipped to withstand a Fed hiking cycle. Central banks are proceeding cautiously with rate cuts even where inflation has slowed, JPMorgan strategists note. That’s keeping real or inflation-adjusted rate differentials elevated across much of the developing world.

In other markets, local factors are offering a buffer. In Hungary, for instance, the new government’s push for euro adoption is drawing investment flows and allowing bond yields to drop nearly two percentage points from this year’s highs. The forint has appreciated more than 4% against the dollar this year.
Elina Theodorakopoulou, a portfolio manager at Manulife Investment Management, said a bigger change is that more investors now see emerging markets as an investment proposition in their own right.
“Higher yields entice more buyers because they offer better risk-adjusted returns,” she said. “That, in general, should keep attracting capital.”

items.title: China and Russia Have Sea, Space and Cyberspace Under Siege
body: Most people don’t realize how profoundly their lives have been shaped by freedom of the commons.

The ability of goods, information and people to move with minimal friction through several crucial, shared domains — seas, skies, space and cyberspace — underpins our global economy. It has facilitated world-changing booms in commerce and prosperity as well as the remarkable great-power peace that has prevailed since 1945. Freedom of the commons is at the heart of the modern world order. It is now, increasingly, under threat.

Freedom of the seas is under assault in waterways from the South China Sea to the Strait of Hormuz. A shifting maritime balance is challenging the US Navy’s role as guardian of the global commons. Space is becoming more crowded and contested — an arena for rivalry in peacetime and perhaps violent conflict in war. Geopolitical tensions are simultaneously fracturing and weaponizing cyberspace as AI-aided tools of cyberwarfare intensify perils.
We’ve entered the era of the contested commons. Domains that once enabled connectivity are becoming battlefields, a change that’s putting the world’s prosperity and progress at risk.

The seas were the original commons. For most of history, they weren’t very free. Pirates ravaged merchant shipping. Countries commissioned privateers to despoil their rivals’ commerce. In the Treaty of Tordesillas, signed in 1494, two great oceanic empires — Spain and Portugal — divided the world’s waters (as well as its newly discovered lands) between themselves.

The rise of free navigation required an intellectual revolution. In 1609, the Dutch scholar Hugo Grotius published his tract Mare Liberum, arguing that the oceans belonged to no sovereign and that all nations should have access to the high seas, even as he acknowledged that states might control territorial waters along their shores. Many powerful actors thought otherwise, so it also took a geopolitical revolution — the rise of Anglo-American supremacy beginning in the 18th century — to make that vision real.

Imperial Britain was an imperfect protector of maritime freedom. Blockade was the Royal Navy’s favored tactic in conflicts; the War of 1812 was essentially an American revolt against London’s heavy-handed naval hegemony. But Britain did have a compelling interest in securing the sea routes that linked its home islands to a growing global empire and its dominant industries to the markets of the world. By the late 19th century, the US was growing rich by trading on oceans pacified by British power. And when British primacy broke down in the 20th century, America stepped up.

In two world wars, Washington fought to subdue the German submarine menace to an open Atlantic. After 1945, America put itself at the center of a world order made stable and prosperous by thriving trade. The US Navy secured sea lanes and protected free navigation in distant oceans. When Libyan dictator Moammar Qaddafi claimed the Gulf of Sidra in the 1980s, when pirates stalked shipping off the Horn of Africa in the 2000s, or when China has challenged the openness of the Western Pacific, Washington has led the response.

By the early 2000s, the US enjoyed what political scientist Barry Posen called “command of the commons.” Dominance of the oceans, air and space allowed the US military to roam the Earth’s far reaches; it provided the security and openness in which go-go globalization could occur.

Global gross domestic product rose (in inflation-adjusted dollars) more than 12-fold between 1950 and 2020. Global trade volumes increased 45-fold over that same period. This would have been impossible had predators ruled the oceans, given that 80% of merchandise trade by volume travels by sea.

Moreover, open oceans had a stabilizing impact on international politics. Countries no longer needed to amass huge, autarkic empires to ensure their prosperity. They could focus on trade and development rather than building massive navies to shield their commerce. For generations, freedom of navigation and great-power peace have reinforced one another. Alas, we’re entering a new era today.

The oldest commons is rife with conflict. The Strait of Hormuz is the world’s energy windpipe; Iran has choked it amid a grinding war against the US. Tehran has used drones, missiles and mines to target the tankers that once carried roughly 20 million barrels of oil through Hormuz daily. The oil that escapes now does so at night, under the protection of the US military and facing persistent attacks by Iran.

Tehran’s tactics have sent fuel prices soaring; economic dislocations may yet affect politics in countries around the world. Yet if the war for Hormuz has been uniquely disruptive, it’s just one episode in a larger trend.

Iran has simply emulated the achievements of the Houthis, who since 2023 have used drones and missiles to sow terror in the Red Sea and force a vast rerouting of global trade. Likewise, Russia’s war on Ukraine made the Black Sea a battleground, sending recurring shocks through food and energy markets. What comes next could be more jarring still.

For years, China has claimed sweeping rights over the South China Sea — through which one-third of global shipping and one-fifth of global trade by value passes — as its sovereign possession. Beijing has built artificial islands and sought to deny other countries’ navies the ability to operate. China is strengthening its presence all around Taiwan, perhaps in preparation for a blockade or quarantine that would interdict some of the world’s most lucrative shipping lanes. Beijing envisions a future in which the Western Pacific is a Chinese lake.

That other great revisionist, Russia, has claimed sovereignty over the Northern Sea Route, which runs through the Arctic Ocean and becomes more attractive as sea lanes around Eurasia’s southern edge grow more contested. In April, Indonesia’s finance minister floated the idea of tolling traffic through the Strait of Malacca, which connects the Indian Ocean to the Pacific. The system of maritime trade has grown “fragile,” warned the Consultative Shipping Group, an organization representing maritime authorities of 18 nations: “Shipping routes are increasingly instruments of leverage and risk.”
Claim by claim, crisis by crisis, we’re glimpsing the return of a more mercantilist world.

That shift at sea is part of a larger geopolitical counterrevolution. In many regions, dissatisfied states are challenging the system Washington created. They’re trying to control oceanic chokepoints as sources of power and leverage. If Iran, Russia or China can grab ahold of key trade routes, they’ll have influence over countries around the world. And as revisionist projects grow more ambitious, America’s naval hegemony has frayed.

Today, the US Navy has fewer than 300 ships. That’s about half of what it had in the 1980s, the last time there was a major Hormuz crisis. Decades of disinvestment have also left the US military with shortages of critical munitions such as Tomahawk missiles it needs to crush the Iranian challenge, let alone beat China in the Pacific. And as President Donald Trump has repeatedly complained, most US allies don’t have the naval punching power to offer much help.

Admittedly, Trump’s periodic threats to seize the Panama Canal or claim Hormuz as US territory haven’t improved the situation. Calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America is trolling with a cost. But the real problem is that the naval balance of power has shifted. China, whose shipyards are churning out warships, is aiming to end Washington’s maritime dominance.

Expect geopolitical rivalry to further fragment the maritime space. The US and China threatened to impose massive port fees on each other’s ships a year ago, a preview of what may come as a harder economic decoupling gradually unfolds. As outlaw nations such as Russia and Iran find their trade more heavily sanctioned, they increasingly use “shadow fleets” — illicit, clandestine networks of vessels — to move their goods around the world.

And from the Baltic Sea to the Taiwan Strait, revisionist states are sabotaging or threatening the submarine cables that provide digital connectivity — an indication of how surging maritime conflict now connects with threats in other domains.

Governments disagree on whether space qualifies as a commons. What’s incontestable is that it is an essential, shared domain. Satellite communications enable precise maritime logistics, split-second financial transactions and other aspects of global connectivity. The US military has long relied on a vast satellite architecture. Yet space has become another area where comfortable assumptions are under strain.

The surging power, again, is China. Beijing has launched more than 1,000 satellites over the past decade, part of a breakneck expansion of its military and commercial networks. It is seeking to displace the supremacy of America’s Global Positioning System with BeiDou, its space-based alternative.

Last year, the head of the US Space Force described Beijing’s progress as “mind-boggling.” China’s sophistication in satellites and reusable rockets rivals and in some cases exceeds America’s. Although China nominally supports freedom of space access for all countries, it and other challengers are preparing to at least complicate US use of space in competition and attack it in conflict.

China is developing dogfighting satellites that can disable adversary satellites in wartime. For situations short of outright conflict, Beijing is unveiling antisatellite capabilities that use non-kinetic methods, such as jamming or dazzling with lasers. The proprietary approach that Beijing takes to the seas could reach into the cosmos. Some Chinese experts argue that the country’s “sovereign airspace could be extended into outer space.”

Russia, too, has periodically interfered with US satellites; it has considered placing nuclear weapons in orbit, with an eye to devastating American satellite clusters if war breaks out. Both Russia and China have carried out direct-ascent antisatellite tests, which create dangerous debris fields. Former US Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense Abraham Denmark called such debris the greatest threat to “the continued openness of the space commons.”

As a manmade domain that is largely in private hands, cyberspace is a different sort of commons — but it’s a critical medium nonetheless. Cyberspace is intimately tied to the space and maritime commons: Fiber-optic cables that carry digital data traffic run across the seabed, while satellite networks enable internet communication. It consists of the vital information networks on which the modern world relies.

This domain, too, was traditionally characterized by American dominance: The internet grew out of a Pentagon project and the US has long used its centrality in global information networks for intelligence snooping and other geopolitical activities.

Yet the US vision of a free and open internet has been in retreat for roughly a generation. China isolated its internet with the so-called Great Firewall; many authoritarian states are asserting doctrines of cyber sovereignty that help them repress and surveil. In 2025, Freedom House found that global internet freedom has declined for 15 straight years. At the same time, middle powers such as Nigeria and Singapore are enacting laws to exert greater control over their online space. The global push for data sovereignty, stricter national control of a country’s digital data, is gaining force.

At the same time, cyberspace has become a domain of lawlessness and coercion. Piracy now afflicts the web more than the waves, in the form of ransomware and other money-seeking attacks. The US government estimates that cybercrime could cost the world $23 trillion annually by next year.

Cyberattacks by shadowy, possibly state-linked actors regularly disrupt the physical world: The Colonial Pipeline attack in 2021, reportedly carried out by a Russian criminal organization, led to gas shortages on the US East Coast. Governments are becoming more aggressive in exploiting their opponents’ cyber-vulnerabilities.

In recent years, China has carried out sophisticated hacks of US telecom companies and critical infrastructure — the latter reportedly a way of gaining leverage ahead of a potential fight over Taiwan. Iran has conducted cyberattacks against US water infrastructure for years. A domain that once seemed to favor freedom and progress has become increasingly fragmented and fierce.

If anything, cyber fights are about to get uglier. New AI models offer some superhuman cyberwarfare capabilities. They may turbocharge conflict between rival powers; their proliferation will also allow terrorists and criminals to conduct sharper, more damaging strikes.

In its latest annual threat assessment, CrowdStrike wrote that “AI-enabled adversaries increased attacks by 89% year-over-year.” To cope, cyber defenses will also have to become faster and more automated. The future of cyberspace will be unforgiving. Or perhaps it will bring blasts from the past.

In August, the White House issued a directive allowing private-sector firms to conduct defensive and offensive operations against foreign cybercriminals, provided they do so under contract with the US government. The rationale is that many US firms have impressive cyber capabilities, while America’s governmental cyberwarriors have their hands full defending official systems and battling state adversaries.

The initiative has been called a “cyber letters of marque” program — a throwback to when countries warred in contested sea lanes by enlisting privateers. Perhaps the future of key domains will resemble a more chaotic past.
We’re still short of the worst-case scenario. Rivalry and violence are roiling the global commons. A great-power war might just rip them apart.

A US-China war in the Western Pacific could make today’s disruptions seem trivial, if Beijing and Washington conduct dueling blockades of Taiwan and the Malacca Strait. Missile salvos and naval combat in the Western Pacific could sever vital trade routes. Combat in space would be intense, as the US and China target each other’s satellite constellations, causing catastrophic disruptions to global connectivity. The two sides might employ strategic cyberattacks meant to cripple each other’s ability to mobilize — and sow cyber chaos in the process. Another vital commons — the air — would be heavily impacted by a war fought over the Western Pacific and, perhaps, parts of the Arctic. As in World War I or World War II, the commons could be scenes of carnage.

Even if this nightmare doesn’t materialize, the years ahead will make us nostalgic for the easy global connectivity of the post-Cold War era. Maritime disputes and chokepoint blockages will likely become more common, as competition intensifies and the maritime balance shifts. States may have to secure their trade routes and sea lanes if US maritime primacy keeps eroding.
The costs for nations and businesses will rise as cybercrime gets more advanced and risks to space-based communications grow. The need for heavy investments in resilience will become more pressing.

Freedom of the commons isn’t the natural state of things. Like the ascent of democracy, the supremacy of free trade and other features of the post-1945 order, it was the creation of a particular geopolitical moment and a particular balance of power. It transformed the lives of people around the globe in ways both historic and too little understood. But today, the balance of power is shifting; the post-1945 order is eroding. We may soon learn what happens when freedom of the commons is lost.
Brands is also a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, the author of The Landscape of Power: Geography and the Rise and Fall of Nations, and a senior adviser to Macro Advisory Partners.

items.title: Congress Should Follow California's Lead on AI Laws
body: They called him a “doomer,” a “decel” and an “alarmist” who was too “focused on science fiction.” Turns out, Scott Wiener, the California state senator behind some of the country’s first safety regulations on artificial intelligence, was a Cassandra. All of a sudden, it appears he’s in good company.

Rocked by an AI researcher’s warning that his former employers Anthropic and OpenAI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” by “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence,” dozens of Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill are now falling all over themselves to regulate advanced frontier models. AI executives calling for a global slowdown in developing the technology isn’t enough.

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont wants to somehow ban artificial superintelligence altogether. Representative Ro Khanna of California wants to create a new federal agency to regulate it, similar to the way we regulate nuclear energy. Others want to form committees, launch investigations, pass legislation and even hold a special session focused on AI.

Whether any of this happens remains to be seen, but a healthy amount of skepticism of the big political promises being made is warranted. Congress has a terrible track record when it comes to trying to regulate AI. Plus, President Donald Trump, likely influenced by his allies in Silicon Valley, is more focused on beating China than on preventing human extinction. “It's going to be fine,” he recently insisted.

But if Congress is serious, then its members should look to California. There are insights and ideas that can — and should — be gleaned from the state where many of the current policy discussions actually began.

Wiener, who is in a tight race to succeed retiring Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi in San Francisco’s 11th Congressional District, introduced his first bill on AI safety two years ago, after researchers in his district made the same sort of doomsday predictions that have so alarmed Americans in recent days.

He proposed mandating so-called “kill switches” to shut down AI models when they fall into the wrong hands or go rogue, like during the notorious Hugging Face incident. And more importantly, the bill would’ve ensured that AI companies could be held legally liable for harms caused by their advanced models. Both of these policies are now wisely being discussed at the federal level.

The goal of his bill, Wiener told me last week, was to mitigate “the very tangible risk” of unchecked AI “facilitating and creating nuclear, biological and chemical weapons; creating novel viruses to trigger pandemics; shutting down the electric system; melting down the financial system — all events that would do massive harm to society.”

Of course, two years ago, with seemingly harmless ChatGPT all the rage, such talk was dismissed by many in government and the broader American public as pure science fiction. So California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed Wiener’s bill, with the backing of some in the state’s congressional delegation, including Khanna (who now says he was wrong).

Newsom, who has long walked a fine line between indulging Silicon Valley and regulating it, explained that he wanted to protect “against actual threats without unnecessarily thwarting the promise of this technology to advance the public good.”

Wiener called it “a setback for everyone who believes in oversight of massive corporations that are making critical decisions that affect the safety and welfare of the public and the future of the planet.” (Hard to argue with him, given that only last week, Anthropic reported that hackers from several restricted countries gained access to its AI agent, Claude, to try designing advanced weapons, researching deadly pathogens and mounting digital surveillance campaigns.)

A year later, Newsom did sign another bill by Wiener, this one also groundbreaking for AI safety, but more focused on transparency. It requires companies to disclose their safety protocols, for instance. Since then, New York, Illinois and a handful of other states have used the bill as a blueprint for their own legislation.

Going forward, Wiener is more bullish than I am about action at the federal level. He backs several of the proposals under discussion, including requirements for “kill switches” and imposing legal liability on AI companies, in hopes of deterring reckless decision-making.

Wiener also echoes Khanna in calling for a new federal regulatory agency that would be “strong and empowered.” But he cautions that true AI safety will mean collaboration with China, so there needs to be an international agency too.
“You need to have a regulator that can keep up with the pace of tech innovation and can take nimble action,” he said. “More nimble than, say, a legislative process.”

And lastly, Wiener said he wants to see mandated third-party auditing — something that has gotten less attention on Capitol Hill, but he would likely push for if elected to the House in November. California is already moving forward. Last week, Newsom signed bills that will create a registry of state-approved auditors and establish criteria for assessing their expertise in calculating risks from AI.

No longer concerned about being cast as a Cassandra, Wiener is blunt that whatever federal lawmakers do, they must act quickly. “What led us to propose these policies, which I wish we had today, were these risks,” he said. “The public is now getting more transparency into this reality, and so that’s a good thing because that lays the groundwork for actually tackling the issue.”
AI killing us all by the end of the decade should be quite the motivator.

items.title: IPhone Duo: A Device for People Who Can't Type
body: This is Bloomberg Opinion Today, a treasure-hunt feel of Bloomberg Opinion’s opinions. On Sundays, we look at the major themes of the week past and how they will define the week ahead. Sign up for the daily newsletter here.

I failed typing class in high school, and I’ve only gotten worse since. One might think that would hamper my career, given that I make my living typing. If we were back in the Underwood era, I’d probably have become a lawyer or a baker or a traffic psychologist.1 But I muddle through, thanks to modern technology and the backspace key. The other key I frequently make use of is the (forward) delete key. At least I do on my company-issued laptop because it’s a Windows machine — corporate, uncool and pretty darn functional. But, deluded snob that I am, I personally live in the Apple universe, where I get luxurious minimalism (thanks, Jony Ive), a credit card without a number on it (thanks a whole lot, Jony Ive) and no forward delete key.

Yes, I know, you can use Fn+Delete. Sure. My fingers can barely find the space bar and I’m supposed to somehow get my pinkie over to the Fn key? Actually, pinkie is just a guess — I have no idea what or where the Fn key is, nonetheless what Fn stands for. Nope, I’ll very slowly move my cursor one step forward for every step back all day long. Because, Apple.

And if I have that much trouble on a MacBook, just imagine me on my iPhone, hunting and pecking and and backing up and being laughed at by my children because I don’t use both thumbs. You know what I miss? My BlackBerry.2 That was the perfect little keyboard, slanted keys with big bumps on them that let your fingers know where they were walking.  But BlackBerrys (yes, proper plural) went the way the of the Nokia ages ago.

What I’ve longed for ever since was an iPhone I could actually type on —  with a keyboard twice the size of my Pro Max’s and text big enough for my fading eyesight, and yet small enough for my pocket. What I wanted was a cool version of the foldable Samsung Galaxy Z. And on Oct. 23, for the little matter of $2,000 and standing in a very long line, I’m getting it: the iPhone Duo.
I don’t need one, but I want one. (Hint: That is the theme of today’s newsletter.)
But will it be creaseless?

“In the foldables market, as with larger smartphones, Samsung again made its move much earlier, offering a foldable Galaxy since 2019,” writes Dave Lee. “Apple’s competitors in China have their own, well-received offerings. In that time, those companies have made great strides in refining the technology, seeking to address the primary and persistent complaint of a crease that emerges down the center of the folded screen. Has Apple solved that problem?”3

Also wanted: A ride in a Cybercab. Not needed: A steering wheel! Elon Musk’s rather lame launch of the vehicle, gullwing doors and all, made for an unflattering comparison. “Musk has been compared to Apple’s legendary co-founder Steve Jobs, not least in terms of their talent for rallying a congregation around some new, futuristic product,” Liam Denning explains. “The difference, however, lies in the ability of Jobs, and his successors, to deliver futuristic and, crucially, highly profitable products ... Both companies inspire, but one is far more of a religious experience than the other.”

Something else you don’t really need but want: an AI agent. You may, of course, not know that you want an AI agent. But you do: As one venture capitalist told Parmy Olson, “Apps and SaaS dead ... AI and agentic hot.”

So if AI’s hot, is Apple still cool? “New releases on Apple Inc.’s App Store surged by about 80% earlier this year,” Parmy writes. “But follow the money in Silicon Valley and something strange is happening: Mobile apps are disappearing from some of tech’s most promising startups. AI is the reason for that, too.”

You may not think you need a Gucci handbag. But you do — if you shop at ... TJ Maxx?? “The discount retailer, with its treasure-hunt feel, might seem anathema to the exclusive, rarefied world of luxury,” writes Andrea Felsted. “But after pushing up prices amid the 2020-2023 boom, designers are struggling to connect with consumers who are financially comfortable enough to splurge on the occasional luxe treat, but not actually rich.”
Something else you want but don’t need — if you live in London anyway — is one of these cuties:

Those are onigiri, plump triangles of rice wrapped in roasted seaweed, and Howard Chua-Eoan calls them the perfect solution for that sudden hunger pang. And now he can get them at ... Marks & Spencer? Howard’s judgment:  “At M&S, which introduced its Kando brand in the spring of 2025, the snack is encased in a plastic case that gives off toolkit vibes,” but “despite these shortcomings, I find this British foray into onigiri quite heartening.”
Now comes the turn: things you need but don’t really want. Like, say, a roof over your head?

“Britons are souring on apartments. That’s a particular problem for London, where flats overwhelmingly account for new-home sales and construction has already slowed to a crawl, leaving housing supply at a fraction of government-set targets,” writes Matthew Brooker. “The many factors at play here include: elevated mortgage rates, which have squeezed affordability for first-time buyers who are the main source of demand for new-build apartments ... but one fundamental driver that shouldn’t be overlooked is the toxic stigma from the country’s leasehold system.”

Then comes the ultimate need not want: eating your peas. “If the 2024 election turned on the price of eggs, the 2026 midterm may well turn on the price of the rest of what’s in Americans’ shopping carts. And 2028 could shape up the same way: According to forecasts, eating is going to get more expensive for at least another year,” writes Mary Ellen Klas. “Congress can demand that the White House stop making the problem worse. The war with Iran, tariffs and the deportation of agricultural workers have led to price pressures that will reverberate through the food supply chain for months to come.”

Finally, you may not want a Terminal High Altitude Area Defense ballistic missile interceptor, but if you want to stay safe in an uncertain world, you need a whole lot of them. “The US still maintains the world’s most powerful military. Those unmatched capabilities provide deterrence, global influence and economic prosperity. There’s just one problem: We’re running out of bullets,” writes David M. Drucker. “This challenge is hardly the fault of this Congress, or this president, alone. But it does exist, and it is jeopardizing military readiness, limiting America’s strategic options and limiting — to borrow Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s favorite word — lethality.”
Pete Hegseth. That name alone has me searching for the Fn+delete key.
Bonus You Can’t Always Get What You Want Reading:
What’s the World Got in Store?
So is there anything in the world you both want and need? Well, in my family, it’s this:
Yep, nothing is worth more to us than an utterly worthless piece of paper.

“The NFL’s fandom is hard to shake because of how it’s developed. In Green Bay, for example, people ‘inherit’ the Packers from their families, share their victories and defeats with their community, and embrace being a “cheesehead” as a personal brand,” Adam Minter explains. “Fans even pay for stadium renovations out of their own pockets (under the guise of valueless shares).”
Meanwhile, in the season’s opening week, fans elsewhere are getting schnookered.

“For years, the league has slowly made NFL football less convenient and affordable to follow. Fans complain, then figure it out, refusing to let the cost of another subscription keep them away from their favorite teams,” writes Adam. “Roger Goodell, the league’s commissioner since 2006, has counted on that reaction, and NFL owners have clearly liked the results. Over the weekend, they rewarded him with a four-year contract extension. They have plenty of reasons to be happy, from a big media rights deal to labor stability. But Goodell’s record also exhibits an uncanny ability to figure out how much change fans can tolerate while still coming back for the next game. The question for Goodell’s next four years is how much further he can push fans before they prove his instincts wrong.”
Yeah, he may do something really silly, like forcing the Rams and Niners to play a game in Australia ...

items.title: Dubai, Abu Dhabi Residents Return to a New Normal: 'Neither War, Nor Peace'
body: Every year, a summer lull in the United Arab Emirates gives way to a September rush. Offices fill up, school buses ferry children through city streets once again, hotels prepare for tourists chasing winter sun while professionals swarm to conferences across the country.

This year, the ritual will test the resilience of the UAE’s post-pandemic boom and whether low taxes and an attractive lifestyle can keep drawing people and capital amid a war that’s showing few signs of resolution. For now, its business as usual in parts of the economy.

Abu Dhabi’s wealth funds are still putting billions to work, encouraging Wall Street banks to add more Gulf staff, while the rush of hedge funds continues. Malls across Dubai and Abu Dhabi are packed with residents chasing “back to school” offers, and restaurants have remained busy.

Still, challenges remain as the regional conflict stretches into its seventh month. Continuing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has raised import costs and fuel prices, while straining supply chains. Airport traffic, hotel occupancy and property sales have dropped, and recruiters say they are having to adjust packages to keep attracting the best talent.

Though the intensity of hostilities has abated since the peak of the war, when the Gulf country successfully fended off thousands of projectiles from Tehran, attacks on shipping and Gulf nations continue. The UAE said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters as recently as Aug. 31, prompting a senior adviser to decry “the state of neither war nor peace” and call for a sustainable solution.

Yet hours after that attempted attack, roads around schools in Dubai and Abu Dhabi were jammed with cars as children streamed in for the first day back — an example of how the most significant shock in the country’s history has, so far, not fundamentally disrupted many routines underpinning its economy.

At Brookfield-backed GEMS Education, about 1,800 students relocated when the war began and roughly 700 have returned, Chief Executive Officer Dino Varkey said. He expects 147,000 enrollments this year, 2,000 more than 2025, but cautioned growth may be softer than historic levels.

Dubai-listed Taaleem Holdings PSC has seen enrollment across its private schools rise roughly 7% from the previous academic year to about 19,500. CEO Alan Williamson said its schools were “still seeing demand outstripping supply even in what we would all agree has been a very challenging period.”

Tellingly, seven new private schools opened in Dubai this year, adding 17,000 new places, including branches of international institutions where fees can run as high as about $42,000 a year. Britain’s Harrow and Rugby School have unveiled Dubai campuses this year, while Harrow has plans for an Abu Dhabi branch next year.
There are also signs of broader economic momentum. While the central bank expects GDP growth to slow to 1.7% this year, economists surveyed by Bloomberg now anticipate a rebound of about 7% in 2027.

The UAE’s financial hubs continue to grow, even as competition for global capital intensifies. Singapore and Hong Kong are offering incentives to hedge fund managers, while Greece has recently attracted some big names. Still, Dubai International Financial Centre crossed 10,000 active companies, while Abu Dhabi’s ADGM issued almost 2,000 licenses and added 4,700 workers in the first half of the year.
But the influx appears to be broader than finance. Dubai’s population hit 4.58 million at the end of 2025, and the city added around 200,000 residents this year, according to government figures.
Also Read: London and Dubai Wealth Concerns See Turkey Make a Play for Rich

That increase is showing up in traffic. Activity near DIFC recovered to about 90% of pre-war levels before slipping in August during the school break, according to mobility analytics firm xMap. The rebound was slightly more muted around Palm Jumeirah and Dubai Marina, likely because those areas are more dependent on tourism.

Abu Dhabi’s $2 trillion in sovereign wealth and deep pools of private capital in Dubai have underpinned the relative strength. Officials have rolled out incentives for sectors like tourism and housing, while an uptick in dealmaking from sovereign entities is prompting firms that work with them to add headcount. Many have started offering more generous allowances for housing, return flights and family travel.
Read More: Wall Street Firms Bolster Gulf Teams to Tackle Wartime M&A Surge

“Employers would rather offer a one-off guarantee or relocation protection than bake a temporary geopolitical risk into permanent compensation,” said Greg Agius, Switzerland-based CEO of the eponymous recruitment firm specializing in finance and private banking.

Demand for artificial intelligence talent also remains strong, though international candidates are doing more due diligence before relocating to the region, said Dan Wardle, a recruiter at tech recruitment firm Discovered.

Elsewhere in the Middle East’s fourth-largest economy, growth in parts of the real estate sector is softening. Sales have slowed relative to the boom years that followed the pandemic and some rents have eased. Still, sellers have largely held off on price cuts. Governments have introduced programs to support residents, including flexible monthly rent payments in Dubai and a rent freeze in Abu Dhabi.

Inflation remains a concern, in line with most other economies contending with the global jump in energy costs and disrupted trade. The UAE’s gasoline prices have climbed about 60% since the war began, though they remain significantly below levels in the US and UK. Growth in the UAE’s consumer price index will accelerate to 3.2% in 2026 before easing to 2.3% in 2027, according to the median of 11 economist estimates compiled by Bloomberg.

Ahmed Galal Ismail, the CEO of Dubai-based Majid Al Futtaim, said the conglomerate is navigating a “challenging operating environment,” with hospitality dented by a pullback in tourism and non-food retail facing product availability issues. The group is passing on some higher costs to shoppers, while consumers are delaying big-ticket purchases, he told Bloomberg TV.
Read More: Dubai’s Latest Boom Is Pricing Out the Expats It Once Coveted

Those strains are most acute at Jebel Ali Free Zone and its port, which together account for at least a fifth of Dubai’s GDP. The UAE is now trying to rejig supply chains and develop new export routes, while outlining a multibillion-dollar infrastructure push as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to bypass the waterway.

The conflict has also impacted traffic at Dubai International Airport, which fell by almost a third in the first six months of the year. The hub expects demand to recover later in 2026, but has pushed back its target of 100 million annual passengers.
Read More: Emirates Rebuilds Capacity Even as US-Iran Conflict Drags On

Dubai hotel occupancy fell to about 64% in August from 76% a year earlier, while room rates dropped about 10%, according to Philip Wooller, Middle East and Africa director at CoStar. “That, considering the reduction in international business, is still a remarkable result,” he said.

That’s due in part to a range of incentives on offer, including campaigns offering free medical insurance and visa-free travel for international visitors. Many hotels and restaurants have also targeted residents with staycation deals and discounts to weather the slowdown.

On a late August weekend, the Atlantis hotel’s Aquaventure water park, built on an artificial palm-shaped island, was packed with people enjoying a reprieve from the desert heat. Upmarket restaurants in the city’s DIFC have remained bustling even during the traditionally slow August.
A stronger recovery may partly depend on the full return of international airlines. Most global carriers remain suspended, with Turkish and Indian airlines among the exceptions.
Read More: Middle East Airlines’ Growth Defies War as Capacity Rebounds

Hotel operators are already seeing signs of improvement. Philippe Zuber, CEO of Kerzner International, which operates the Atlantis hotels and One&Only Resorts, said regional demand is being bolstered by a gradual return of international travelers, pushing occupancy across its Dubai properties over 80% for the year-end festive period.

Occupancy will likely get a further boost from conferences rescheduled for the final months of the year after being postponed during the conflict. The period is also typically the UAE’s busiest for tourism, with several high-profile restaurants slated to open in Dubai and Abu Dhabi ahead of the expected pickup.
Read More: Dubai Tourism Slump Hits Hotels, Malls; Recovery Seen in 2H27

December will bring a slate of major events, including the Formula One Abu Dhabi Grand Prix and the opening of the Guggenheim museum. Abu Dhabi Finance Week has also lined up some of the biggest names in global finance for its annual gathering that month.
Beyond the year-end calendar, the UAE’s traditional advantages should continue to draw expatriates, according to Monica Malik, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank.

“The various indicators point to the UAE’s population as remaining,” she said. “A favorable business environment, including low taxes, world class infrastructure and access to labor will continue to stand out in the medium term.”

items.title: Ukraine Says Passenger Train Headed to Warsaw Hit by Drone
body: The locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw was hit by a Russian drone just kilometers from the Polish border on Sunday morning, Ukraine’s foreign minister said, as Moscow’s airstrikes push closer to NATO territory.

The attack happened minutes after another train carrying European officials including former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson left the station on the way back from an annual conference in Kyiv. Ex-CIA director David Petraeus was at the station when the drone hit, according to the New York Times.
The strike marked the latest escalation by Russia in the war — currently in its fifth year — as acts of sabotage, arson and drone incursions proliferate across the continent.
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X, calling for Europe to increase sanctions against Russia.

Ukraine’s state railway operator confirmed a strike on a train in Volyn, about two kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Ukraine-Poland border in northwestern Ukraine. Russian authorities haven’t yet commented.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said there was no violation of the border but called the incident “escalation” by Russian President Vladimir Putin. The drones involved in the incident were Geran-5 jet-powered drones, Polish authorities said.
Read more: Russia’s Hybrid War Is Europe’s Top Threat, EU Commander Warns

Kremlin forces “struck a passenger train locomotive,” the railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Telegram. “The monitoring group warned the train crew about the threat in advance, thanks to which no one was injured.”
The train, which had 208 people aboard, will continue on to Poland after a delay at the border of about six hours, the Polish railways said.
Ukrzaliznytsia said Sunday’s strike was the second this weekend. Sybiha late Saturday posted images of railway facilities struck in Lutsk in northwestern Ukraine and Fastiv, southwest of Kyiv.

“Unable to achieve its goals on the battlefield, Russia attempts to make the entire territory of Ukraine a battlefield and turns to systematic attacks against civilians, trains, and the infrastructure that keeps the country moving,” he said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, speaking after an emergency meeting with top civilian and military leaders, said he can’t exclude the potential of escalation by Russia to Poland’s territories in the next weeks or months, including attempts to disrupt or paralyze border crossings.
Poland will consider how to mobilize allies to be prepared for a common response if needed, he said.
Images on social media also showed a large fire at a gasoline filling station close to the border crossing between Yahodyn in Ukraine and Dorohusk in Poland.
Margus Tsahkna, Estonia’s foreign affairs minister, said on X that members of his team had been “stuck at this very border crossing, unable to leave Ukraine because of the Russian drone threat.”

Separately on Sunday, Vilnius airport was shut down for a time as NATO scrambled fighter jets in response to a possible drone sighting in Lithuanian airspace, Reuters reported. The potential drone was later reported to have been a flock of birds.

items.title: Labour Signals Action Against Farage's Crypto Donation Surge
body: The UK government hit back at record-breaking donations to Reform UK from two crypto billionaires, with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner arguing that Labour’s planned legislation will prevent rich people from “being able to buy their way” in an election.
“If you don’t pay taxes, if you don’t live here, you can’t buy your way into our democracy because you’re a billionaire,” Rayner said on Sunday in an interview on Sky television.

In the past two days Nigel Farage’s Reform party has received two donations totalling £72 million ($97 million) from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and BitMEX founder Ben Delo, far surpassing the funding raised by the rival Labour and Conservative parties so far this year.
The record amounts are designed to help the insurgent party fend off its critics while turbo-charging its attempts to gain power at the next general election.

Parliament is currently debating new legislation that would limit donations from British citizens living overseas to £100,000 annually. Restrictions would also apply to those who have returned to the UK recently.

In a separate BBC interview, Rayner said the new legislation would apply retroactively and that anyone whose donation fell foul of the law would have 60 days to return the money. She said that Labour isn’t opposed in principle to capping all donations, but wants to look at loopholes that would for example allow individuals to donate via various corporate entities.
“It’s not as simple as we’re saying we won’t put a cap” on donations, she told the BBC.
Rayner said that she and another senior UK minister, Louise Haigh, had written to the Electoral Commission to see “what further measures we need to protect our democracy.”

Reform’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said in a BBC interview on Sunday that the Delo and Harborne donations “are entirely in line with the law as it is and as far as we know the law as it’s going to be in the future.”

He said that neither donor had asked for anything in return. “Neither of these two individuals nor anyone who donates to our party, is going to be on some honours list in the years ahead, if we’re lucky enough to be in government.”
Registry filings earlier this year showed that Delo is now usually resident in the UK, after living in Asia for at least the last decade.
The government’s anti-corruption champion Margaret Hodge said the Reform donations raise the question of what changes are needed to the UK rules on political donations.

“I think we’ve got to reflect as this bill passes through Parliament as to what we don’t want our politics in the UK to mirror those of America, where money can buy you greater access, greater influence, and greater control,” she told Bloomberg in an interview.

items.title: Xi Pitches AI Vision at BRICS Summit as China Duels With US
body: Chinese President Xi Jinping has sought to turn the annual BRICS summit into another platform for championing Beijing’s vision for artificial intelligence, as it vies for global influence over the technology with the US.

China will lead the creation of what Xi called a BRICS “community” for open-source AI. Speaking on Sunday in New Delhi, he said the initiative will “support the cooperation in developing and applying large language models,” as well as holding AI seminars and training courses for members of the club of major emerging economies.

A day earlier, Xi welcomed BRICS nations to join a new group of nearly 30 countries set up by Beijing and called the World AI Cooperation Organization. BRICS must “strengthen cooperation in the field of AI, encourage open source, openness, collaboration and sharing,” he said.

Xi is pushing for greater sway as global AI governance becomes a new battleground for the world’s leading powers. Beijing is looking to build an open-source AI ecosystem that offers its citizens and global customers a cheaper alternative to US technology, while American developers including OpenAI and Anthropic prefer closed models.
For now, it wasn’t immediately clear if China’s vision is winning favor from other BRICS members such as the United Arab Emirates and India.

A joint declaration issued by the group on Saturday didn’t explicitly address Xi’s pitch. Instead, it called for “international cooperation in enhancing accessibility of AI resources while ensuring its safety, security, inclusiveness and reliability.”

Beijing will likely push for AI governance again when it hosts the BRICS Summit in 2027. State media has suggested that next year’s focus will be on topics including AI, digital economy and green development.
China’s open-source approach was also invoked by State Security Minister Chen Yixin as a way to ensure AI security and equity.

Certain countries are using blacklists, closed-source ecosystems, and tech curbs to “sever global AI industrial chains and supply chains, exacerbating the imbalanced development of the global AI industry,” Chen wrote in a journal article made public Saturday.
Still, Beijing also maintains there’s a limit to openness.

Xi emphasized the need to balance development and security at his debut appearance at China’s top AI summit in July. A social media account frequently used to signal official policy thinking has said China should restrict access to the most powerful features of artificial intelligence models.

items.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Refineries as Odesa Ports Targeted
body: Russia hit energy facilities and other sites in the Odesa region in southern Ukraine overnight while Kyiv’s forces claimed strikes on oil refineries in southern Russia and Tatarstan.

Debate continues on when and where new talks may be scheduled on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine, well into its fifth year, after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv last weekend for top-level meetings.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said on Telegram post that its forces struck power substations in Odesa and Mykolaiv that support port infrastructure in the regions. A logistics center in Nova Poshta was also hit in Odesa region. In addition, railway infrastructure in western Ukraine used to transport military cargo from European countries was targeted, Russia said. It also struck a dry cargo ship carrying supplies for the Ukrainian Armed Forces in the port of Odesa, the ministry reported late Sunday. Ukraine hasn’t commented.

A multi-storey apartment building, private homes, two educational institutions, and infrastructure facilities were damaged during Russia’s overnight attacks, Serhiy Lysak, head of the Odesa military administration, said in a statement. The consequences of the attack are being assessed.
Russia has turned to “systematic attacks against civilians, trains and the infrastructure that keeps the country moving,” Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
On Saturday, Ukrainian tennis player Dayana Yastremska posted on Instagram that her family’s apartment in an Odesa high-rise had been destroyed by a Russian Kalibr cruise missile.
Russia’s Defense Ministry on Sunday also reported movement in the ground war, saying its forces were expanding an “outer control zone” in the Kharkiv region in northern Ukraine, Interfax reported.

Ukraine’s General Staff said in an X post that the Slavyansk oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region and the Taneco refinery in Tatarstan were hit overnight, along with a site at Millerovo in the Rostov region used for the storage and launch of drones.

Regional authorities had earlier cited damage to unspecified industrial and civilian facilities in the Nizhnekamsk region of Tatarstan, a major oil-refining and petrochemical hub located about 900 kilometers (560 miles) east of Moscow, Interfax reported.
A blaze was also reported at a facility in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia’s Krasnodar region following a Ukrainian drone attack, Interfax reported, citing regional authorities.

The General Staff also said it has established that a previously-reported strike on the Saratov oil refinery in southwestern Russia damaged the primary crude oil distillation unit and a section of the main oil pipeline. Ukraine has struck the Rosneft PJSC facility several times in the past.

Also since Saturday evening, Ukrainian drones have targeted the training and education center of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Russian-occupied southeastern Ukraine more than ten times, Interfax reported citing the plant’s spokesperson.
The claims can’t be independently verified.

Russia said its air defenses intercepted 389 Ukrainian drones across multiple regions. Ukraine shot down 405 out of 453 Russian drones across multiple locations overnight, according to preliminary data from Ukraine’s General Staff.
Read more: Zelenskyy Floats Idea of Putin Meeting at Trump’s G20 Summit

In an interview with Germany’s DW published on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would travel to Miami for President Donald Trump’s G20 leaders’ summit in mid-December if Vladimir Putin also attended, saying the two leaders should meet and make decisions.

Zelenskyy said in Canada last week that new meetings could be held with US envoys in New York late this month, potentially when world leaders gather for the UN General Assembly’s general debate. Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s presidential office, later said that a new round of trilateral talks — involving Ukraine, Russia and the US — may come in October.

A number of issues must be resolved before any trilateral meeting can take place, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov, who’s accompanying Putin at the BRICS summit in New Delhi, told Russia’s Izvestia newspaper. The “territorial issue” remains key to progress, he added.

Putin insists Ukraine must surrender the remainder of its eastern Donetsk region as part of any deal to end the war. Ukraine has repeatedly rejected the demand to hand that region, which Russian forces have failed to capture in fighting dating back to 2014.

“I would say the demands remain the same; there has been no tightening. We would simply like them to be met sooner or later — preferably sooner,” Ushakov said in a separate comment to state TV reporter Pavel Zarubin.
