items.title: How Likely Is It That AI Kills Us All?
body: Welcome back to The Forecast from Bloomberg Weekend, where we help you think about the future — from next week to next decade.
This weekend we have another special issue: all about drones and what they tell us about the future of warfare. But first: Just how likely is it that AI kills us all?

If drones and AI doom aren’t for you, you can read about why high yields aren’t going anywhere, how therapists are experimenting with creating AI twins and the growing post-exit ecosystem helping founders deal with their unexpected wealth. Otherwise, here’s what we’ve got for you:

Is the world hurtling toward an AI catastrophe? For years, experts in and around the industry have warned that we may be — a view encapsulated, in extreme form, by the 2025 book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, by the AI researchers Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares.

But for most of the past two years it seemed as if the doomers were losing the argument. Yes, models were exhibiting some worrisome tendencies — like a penchant for scheming — but most of the attention was on the economic potential and risks.

The last two months may be remembered as the moment when the doomers’ fears broke through into the public consciousness. In late July, OpenAI disclosed that its models had hacked the AI company HuggingFace during a testing exercise — unbeknownst to the OpenAI researchers running the test. Other model providers soon disclosed that they’d had similar experiences. OpenAI and the independent research group METR added new, worrisome details — not only about gaps in OpenAI’s testing procedures, but also outlining how hundreds of AI agents coordinated with each other to access the open internet.

Last week, OpenAI released its latest model, Astra, and president Greg Brockman suggested it might mark the beginning of the “AGI” era. This past week, an Anthropic researcher resigned, saying that the frontier AI companies were “gambling with our lives.” In response, a current Anthropic employee and head of one of its safety research groups posted publicly that he thought there was a greater than 10% chance that AI would kill all humans “within the next decade.” OpenAI head Sam Altman told staff that he was open to slowing the company’s pace of development. On Saturday, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post calling for a slowdown as well as for third-party model evaluators. The doomers had reentered the chat.

“Safety is becoming a more immediate constraint on frontier [AI] development,” wrote Michael Deng, a geoeconomics analyst at Bloomberg Economics. OpenAI claims its latest model is safer than previous ones, he notes, but it may be less transparent, too. (Link for Terminal subscribers only.)

Let’s cut to the chase: Are we all going to die at the hands of AI? The best answer is unsatisfying: Nobody knows. The second best answer, though, is: Probably not, but the chances are still uncomfortably high.

It’s impossible to predict anything about AI too confidently, but the best attempt I know of is the Forecasting Research Institute’s polls of AI experts and forecasters. (One of the researchers behind it, psychologist Philip Tetlock, explained the spirit of the project in Bloomberg Weekend late last year.) In short, the project asks experts, seasoned forecasters and the public to make concrete, quantifiable predictions about AI — and measures their progress over time.

In late spring, they asked about the chance of an AI catastrophe that killed at least 10% of the population. The median AI expert predicted a 0.3% chance of that happening by 2030, 2% by 2050 and 5% by the end of the century.

The forecasters, who are used to putting probabilities on things and being scored on their results, are notably less worried. The median “superforecaster” put a 0.1% risk of catastrophe by 2030, 0.88% by 2050 and 2.4% by 2100.

If you’re looking for a dose of optimism, there it is: Trained forecasters do not, as a group, share the AI community’s level of alarm. But a 1-in-1000 chance that AI kills 10% of humanity in the next four years is hardly comforting. And, as AI-and-labor researcher Molly Kinder noted in a recent Substack, we regularly go out of our way to avoid risks that are far less likely and less harmful than that.

In their report, the FRI researchers note one key area of consensus. “Both optimistic and pessimistic forecasters agreed” that the risk would be substantially lower if AI capabilities progressed more slowly so society had a chance to catch up. When asked to assume “rapid” progress in AI, the probabilities offered by both groups roughly doubled. (We wrote about a similar project from MIT in July.)

How might AI kill so many people? Participants in FRI’s forecasts mentioned engineered pathogens, autonomous weapons, or AI-induced nuclear escalation — as well as the more sci-fi possibility of a rogue AI turning on humanity.

For some of the “optimists” — those putting a lower probability on AI catastrophe — the most likely scenarios for mass casualties remain the ones we’re used to, and the ones that we control. “The most plausible pathways to losses on that scale,” one participant wrote, “would likely involve human decisions… even if AI played a supporting role.”
— Walter Frick, Bloomberg Weekend
(Disclosure: I was previously a contributing editor at FRI.)

The southern Ukrainian city of Kherson delivers a dystopian vision of what happens when drones attack an urban center. There are more than 5,000 Russian drone attacks there every week. The military shoots down the vast majority of them, but the few that get through are enough to reap death, destruction and an exodus of civilians.

Kherson’s situation is extreme and tragic. But more and more cities are being forced to think about how they would defend against drones if they had to. And no one has a perfect answer yet. Earlier this year, Iranian drones struck Dubai, Kuwait City and Bahrain’s capital, Manama. This summer, Romania shot down its fourth Russian drone, Germany blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport and Latvia blamed Russian jamming for a Ukrainian drone that strayed into its airspace.

Defense firms have been experimenting with how to stop drones on the battlefield — employing interceptors, microwaves and even lasers. But when it comes to urban areas, the counter drone challenge is complicated by the presence of civilians and tall buildings. “You also don’t want to necessarily blast a direct energy weapon wildly across a city,” says Gregory Falco, director of the Aerospace Adversary Lab at Cornell University. “Unless of course you have a score to settle with someone living in the high rise you just lasered”.

Right now, there is no consensus on how to defend civilian populations from drones. Governments are still debating: Is the risk of falling debris worth it to intercept a drone whose target is unclear? How many $4 million missiles can you justify firing at drones that cost just tens of thousands of dollars? Even as Kyiv’s counter-drone system struggles against Moscow’s new jet-powered drones, it is considered the gold standard of city air defense. But this is also not an off-the-shelf system other countries can copy. Every counter-drone system needs to be tailored to a specific location so, for example, drones can be shot down over uninhabited areas.

In Kherson, so far, it is the low-tech methods that have proven most effective at protecting those who remain, says Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson state administration. Today much of the local region is draped with green-tinged nets. “Our experience has shown that when you are under the net, you’re as protected as practical solutions can make you,” he says. Tolokonnikov has been travelling Europe to talk about what other countries can learn from Kherson’s experience. His conclusions: Europe is not ready for the new drone threat. “In many cases, they don’t even plan to be prepared.”
— Morgan Meaker, Bloomberg Weekend

Drones will reshape the sound of war. In conflicts around the world, the cracks and booms of explosions are now accompanied by the dzzzzzz of drones overhead. More drones doesn’t only mean more buzzing but also more phone alerts, more sirens, more explosions, more roaring generators and more grinding machinery clawing through rubble. — Morgan Meaker and Simon  Marks, Bloomberg Weekend

Killer drone swarms are coming. On a quiet Maryland farm, a startup is testing drone swarms that could, if allowed, act autonomously. Operating in a mode called “terminal guidance,” five quadcopter drones move towards a tank in a ‘V’ formation. With each of them locked onto their allocated pixels, if the tank moves, so will they. — Katrina Manson, Bloomberg News

Russian attacks on Kyiv could be about to get worse. Ukrainian authorities are expecting Russia to increase its attacks using jet-powered drones, a new iteration of drone Kyiv finds difficult to intercept. That could be part of a strategy of stockpiling rockets for use this winter. — Volodymyr Verbianyi and Olesia Safronova, Bloomberg News

Europe’s third wave of military spending will boost software makers. Shares of the small Swedish company Mildef, which makes rugged laptops, servers and computer screens for armored vehicles, have risen more than 80% so far this year as it starts to feel the benefits of… military spending that’s focused more on computer systems and drones than tanks and ammunition. — Jonas Ekblom and Isolde MacDonogh, Bloomberg News

Kyiv’s drone attacks on Russian industry are expanding. This week Ukraine said its drones hit two gas condensate processing plants in Russia’s Arctic zone for the first time. The attack, which took place ahead of Russian parliamentary elections later this month, was the deepest inside Russia so far, Ukrainian special forces said on Telegram, with the machines traveling more than 3,000km to reach their targets.

New Trump tariffs will test US drone makers. The White House is applying a tariff on imports of unmanned aircraft systems to reduce the industry’s reliance on foreign-made critical components. This will test whether protectionism can pave the way for onshoring an industry. — Thomas Black, Bloomberg Opinion

... the search for GPS alternativesGPS spoofing and other countermeasures meant to knock drones from the skies over battlefields are giving rise to novel navigation systems that will work even in the face of intense jamming. Australian company Q-CTRL uses quantum measurements of the earth’s magnetic and gravitational fields to keep uncrewed systems on course in jammed or otherwise GPS-denied environments. ASIO, an Israeli company, navigates with onboard cameras and image processing.

Although GPS remains the gold standard, having other systems that can get near a target is sufficient in many situations. Most systems will also combine several guidance methods. “The technology is not a replacement for GPS,” says Charlie Burnard, Q-CTRL’s global head of government engagement. “It is a reliable, resilient backup for environments where GPS or even other navigation modalities just don’t operate.” — Gerry Doyle, Bloomberg News

Sunday: Sweden holds its general election; the EU meets to discuss its approach to the Arctic region. Monday: Canada holds its inaugural investment summit Investment; G20 energy ministers meet; and the 78th Emmy Awards are held in LA.

Tuesday: China reports property and retail data; CPI data is in from France, Israel, Nigeria, Poland, Saudi Arabia and Spain; UK reports unemployment data; and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testifies in the House.
Wednesday: The UK reports CPI; the Fed decides on interest rates; Snap launches its new Specs AR-glasses.
Thursday: Euro-zone CPI and US housing data are out; BOE decides on rates; London Fashion Week begins.
Friday: Japan reports CPI and decides on rates, Russia holds parliamentary elections, NATO defense chiefs meet.
Have a great Sunday and a productive week.
— Morgan Meaker, Walter Frick, Jackie Bischof and Silvia Killingsworth, Bloomberg Weekend

items.title: UK Tech Spinouts Are Struggling Outside the Golden Triangle
body: Much of the world’s wastewater is still treated using a century-old, energy-intensive process of pumping oxygen through tanks of sewage. Thames Water, the UK’s largest water company, is trialing an alternative developed at Newcastle University that uses microbes and electrodes to break down waste. It both uses less energy and gives off ammonia that can be recovered and sold as fertilizer.

Elizabeth Heidrich came up with the idea in 2012, and when environmental engineer Pavlina Theodosiou joined her lab eight years later they began trying to turn the research into a business. Their company, METzero, spun out of Newcastle in 2024 and has since raised about £750,000 ($1 million) in grants.

Over 2,000 university spinouts have formed in the UK since 2010, with a combined value of about £49 billion — most of them in so-called deep-tech, which originates novel breakthroughs in science and engineering. Successes include Oxford Nanopore, which went public at a £3.4 billion valuation, and Oxford Ionics and OrganOx, which were acquired for more than $1 billion each last year.

Theodosiou said support from government-funded Northern Accelerator, founded in 2016 to help researchers commercialize their work, was vital in the early stages of her endeavor. It allowed her to hire someone to develop METzero’s business plan, while a Royal Academy of Engineering fellowship bought her out of her university contract for a year. “That helped me to make the full transition from lecturer to CEO,” Theodosiou said.

Despite these successes, Britain is increasingly fretting about two key questions of geography: where university spinouts are formed, and where they end up. The concern is that, beyond the so-called Golden Triangle of Oxford, Cambridge and London, innovative research can struggle to make it out of the lab. Worse still, the economic benefits of successful spinouts often go on to leave the country.
“The north east does not lack innovation or founders’ ambitions,” said Theodosiou. “It just lacks that same density of specialist capital.”
The UK is home to three of the world’s top 10 universities and, according to the Royal Academy of Engineering, leads Europe in the creation, funding and value of deep-tech spinouts.

Across the universities in Northern Accelerator’s umbrella, the number of spinouts rose from two in 2018 to 10 in 2025. But that remains well behind the 70-odd coming out of the so-called Golden Triangle of Oxford, Cambridge and London each year.

The Golden Triangle accounted for almost half of UK university spinouts founded between 2013 and 2024, and attracted two-thirds of the venture capital, according to a February report by Tony Hickson, whose career was based in university technology transfer, investment and startups.

Data compiled by Indeed for Bloomberg also show it made over half of the sector’s hiring. That’s despite new ideas germinating across the country, according to the UK’s latest national assessment of university research.

“The UK really cannot maximize its spinout potential if world-class research outside the Golden Triangle lacks the same access to networks, capital and commercialization support,” said Ana Avaliani of the Royal Academy of Engineering.

A second concern is that mature spinouts are, increasingly, leaving Britain altogether. Just 36% of spinouts founded between 2013 and 2024 that went public did so in the UK, down from 79% of those founded before 2013.

PsiQuantum, a quantum-computing spinout from the University of Bristol, moved to the US and was valued at $7 billion in a fundraising round last year. Exscientia, an AI drug-discovery company spun out of the University of Dundee, listed on the Nasdaq in 2021 before merging with US biotech Recursion Pharmaceuticals three years later.

The main reason is the lack of scale-up capital. There’s almost four times more private funding for startups in the US than the UK, but the gap widens to nine times for investments above £100 million, according to figures from the government’s Council for Science and Technology.

There’s also a “persistent technical literacy gap” among British financiers, said Hickson. That’s “most acute among later-stage investors, many of whom lack the scientific expertise needed to assess complex scale-up ventures.”

Deep-tech companies often need to spend heavily developing technology before they can generate revenue, according to Nigel Toon, who co-founded Bristol University spinout Graphcore and is launching a specialist spinout fund.
“That needs investors who can really have very high conviction around the technology and have a deep understanding of the market so that they can see the potential,” Toon said.

The government was reportedly considering an exit tax for university spinouts moving abroad, but quickly ruled out the idea, according to the Financial Times. Critics argued it would penalize successful businesses, without fixing the underlying factors that push them abroad.

“If the government wants more spinouts to remain and grow in Britain, the strongest response is to make the UK the best place for them to raise capital, win customers and scale, not simply to make leaving more expensive,” said METzero’s Theodosiou.
The government said it wants the country “to be one of the best places in the world to start and scale a business,” but declined to comment on policy speculation.

Duncan Ivison, vice chancellor of the University of Manchester, said it’s not always a bad thing when spinouts moves abroad. “If we spin out a billion-pound company from Manchester and they set up in Silicon Valley or in San Francisco, I’m like hallelujah,” he said. “That is fantastic.”

“Of course, we’d love it if they stayed in Manchester and employed people in Manchester, contributed to the UK’s GDP,” Ivison added. “But over time, if you are spinning out billion-pound companies that American, European, Chinese, or Australian investors want to invest in, you must be doing something right. And eventually, good things will come on the back of that.”
The number of UK spinouts has fallen from its pandemic peak, according to the Higher Education Statistics Agency, but there are other signs of improvement.

Founders and investors have long complained that institutions demanded too big a slice, but the average university stake fell to 16% in 2024 from 28% in 2017 following a government review, according to the Royal Academy of Engineering.

And there’s been a proliferation of specialist university finance firms that offer support as well as capital, including Oxford Science Enterprises, which has raised over £800 million from investors, and Northern Gritstone, a cluster of universities in Manchester, Sheffield, Liverpool and Leeds.

“A lot of good work was done under the previous Conservative government that’s been continued under the Labour government, and things have improved a lot,” said James Wise, a partner at Balderton Capital. He said the firm has invested in far more spinouts recently than when he started 15 years ago.

“It’s a very common criticism to say that the UK is lousy at commercializing its high-quality university IP but that story is starting to sound a bit old,” said Ivison, referring to intellectual property by its acronym. “I think we’re beginning to really turn the tide on that.”
After a successful pilot led by Northumbrian Water, METzero’s Theodosiou is hoping to raise £1.5 million by the end of the year, to move METzero into its own premises.
But to get the funding, Theodosiou is planning three trips to London in September. “That’s where the money is,” she said.

items.title: Asia Chip Stocks Drop as AI Chiefs Urge Slower Model Development
body: Asian semiconductor and equipment stocks fell Monday as higher oil prices and calls from major AI leaders to slow model development weighed on sentiment.

Memory names were among the hardest hit, with SK Hynix Inc. and Kioxia Holdings Corp. tumbling more than 6% and 9% each, before paring some losses. Samsung Electronics Co. also declined 4%, while SoftBank Group Corp.’s shares fell the most in nearly three months.

Anthropic PBC’s chief executive officer Dario Amodei said Saturday his company would implement new safety steps and urged the industry to support a downshift. His call was endorsed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and xAI Corp.’s Elon Musk, while US President Donald Trump downplayed such concerns.

The AI slowdown risks are compounding concerns over valuation and momentum, even as analysts stress the longer-term spending case remains strong. Sentiment toward Asian tech firms was further pressured by climbing oil prices on Middle East tensions and firmer bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike this week.

“Investors will undoubtedly be questioning the AI boom’s trajectory this week,” said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at eToro. “Samsung and SK Hynix both falling this morning gives us the early read that investors are selling first and working out the details later.”

Chinese chip stocks and AI models also fell on Monday, though the latter’s moves were driven more by additional share sales. In Hong Kong, Shanghai Biren Technology Co. slid more than 4%. Shares of Z.AI Co. tumbled 10% at one point as it unveiled a $5 billion stock-and-convertible offering.

Even before AI leaders’ call, tech shares have been sluggish as investors questioned whether earnings could justify soaring infrastructure costs. Signs of heavier spending or weaker returns have quickly triggered selloffs, particularly in high‑valuation stocks.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Stock index has dropped more than 4% from the record notched in June, while futures fell 1.3% during Asia’s Monday morning trading.

The AI sector’s newfound caution further dents sentiment, given valuations assume not only strong demand but a relentless pace of model development, Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets in Singapore, said.
Still, Chanana and other market watchers questioned whether the cautious mood would have lasting effects on tech spending or suppliers’ outlooks.
Investment in cybersecurity and AI monitoring tools is set to rise, while cooling and power equipment firms stand to benefit from projects already underway, Chanana said.

Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore, echoed that companies across the global AI supply chain will continue to accelerate, with development still in its early stages.
“I’m not sure the rest of the ecosystem is willing to accept the current pecking order and slow down while the technology continues to evolve so rapidly,” he said.

items.title: Israel Election: Netanyahu Rival Eisenkot Can at Least Promise Less War
body: On Oct. 27 Israel goes to the polls in one of the most fiercely contested elections since the state’s inception in 1948. At stake is the possible displacement of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by an apparently more moderate leader, Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot, a former chief of Israel’s army who has been in politics for only four years, heads a new party named Yashar — Hebrew for honest or upright. This contrasts with Netanyahu, who is still fighting protracted corruption proceedings.

The veteran prime minister, whom I have known, disliked and feared for many decades, has held power since 2009 with only one 18-month interruption. He is running with a doctrine almost unimaginable in any other society. He promises Israeli voters forever war. Netanyahu asserts a right — indeed, a duty — for his nation to take preemptive military action against any perceived threat. He insists on this even though his campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran have cost Israel an estimated $142 billion, about half the national annual budget, and killed a huge number of people, mostly civilians.

After Israel’s victory in the 1967 Six-Day War, there was a Tel Aviv joke: “We’ve got peace. We’ve got a piece of Syria, a piece of Egypt, a piece of Jordan.” Today, another plank in Netanyahu’s electoral platform is his expansion of Israel’s borders through the creation of “security zones” in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, where its forces promise to remain indefinitely.

Expansionism in the West Bank, where more than 200 new settlements and outposts have been established since 2023, is often accompanied by acts of terrorism against Palestinians, committed by ever-more heavily armed settlers. Even US President Donald Trump’s pro-settler ambassador Mike Huckabee has condemned extremist violence.

This week Britain announced economic sanctions against settlement-sourced goods, and other nations including Canada and France are expected to follow suit. It is striking that while many conservatives have condemned the gesture, some liberal Israelis, including former senior officials, endorse the UK action as a justified response to systemic settler assaults.

The terrorization and dispossession of Palestinians by armed and masked militias will assuredly continue. Though Israel’s left-wing opposition talks of expelling most settlers from the West Bank in a peace deal, almost nobody thinks this will happen. Eventual Israeli annexation looks inevitable to me.

The big question is whether an election defeat for Netanyahu would change the thrust of Israeli policy, driven by his doctrine that might is right, and reinforced by the enduring — and justified — outrage generated by the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas massacre of 1,200 Israelis.

Eisenkot’s language is less bellicose than that of the incumbent. Since 2023 he has condemned Netanyahu’s vacuous promises of “total victory” over Hamas, dismissing them as unattainable. His election pitch is that of an honest man who will end the wars that oblige several hundred thousand Israeli reservists to perform more than 100 days of military service a year, amid a chronic shortage of regular troops. The candidate’s youngest son Gal was killed, aged 25, in a 2023 special-forces operation in Gaza. Eisenkot quit Netanyahu’s war cabinet in disgust within months of being appointed during the post-Oct. 7 crisis.

Yet few people in Israel, or among Middle East-watchers abroad including me, are optimistic about the prospects for a radical change of direction, should Eisenkot win. Many Israelis hate Netanyahu, and deplore his avarice. Since 2023, however, the mood of the country has become more hawkish. Polls show solid support for ruthlessness toward the Palestinians.

Only a small minority of liberals, and the courageous newspaper Ha’aretz, fully reckon with the settler attacks, and criticize the armed forces and police for consistently refusing to intervene, except on the side of the antagonists. In this election campaign Yair Golan, leader of the small Democrat party, is the sole advocate of dialogue with the Palestinians.

Although Israel is a cosmopolitan society, for years its voters have been turning in upon themselves. The lesson they take from history is that they can depend upon no one save themselves, in peace or war. When liberal critics highlight the cost of Netanyahu to their country’s global standing, plenty of Israelis shrug.

The only foreign relationships that appear to matter to the political establishment are those with the US, and with their Republican and Christian evangelical supporters there. While backing is flagging among American Jews and in the US at large, MAGA is still squarely behind Israel.

Trump nurses a grievance against Netanyahu for persuading him that a joint assault on Iran would achieve easy success. But there is no hint that he will cut off military or financial backing for Israel. Sentimental British people still sometimes talk nonsense about the UK’s alleged special relationship with the US. In truth, for many years America’s most important tie has been with Israel, whether its under Republican or Democrat rule. And so it remains.

Washington foreign-policy gurus strive to persuade presidents — not just Trump — that Americans pay a high price for their blank check. But there seems no realistic prospect that US policy will change radically, even after 2028.

Israelis are perceived by most of the American right as “people like us,” winners, while Arabs and especially Palestinians are viewed as alien — and losers. MAGA supporters, taking their cue from the president, do not do compassion. The inhabitants of the West Bank possess neither the power nor riches to advance a successful claim upon their sympathy.
On the topic of backing winners, polls suggest that Netanyahu may well lose this election. But he is working overtime to ensure that any alternative coalition faces big difficulties in governing.
And those of us abroad who wish the best for Eisenkot, or for any new leader who seeks to lower Israel’s mailed fist, have to acknowledge the huge difficulties of stopping the forever wars.

The so-called two-state solution is as dead as the Egyptian pharaohs, and every dove who wishes to seem credible should admit this. Those of us who have witnessed at first hand the brutal ruthlessness with which the Israelis administer their occupied territories find it hard to imagine how Palestinians can be peacefully reconciled with their neighbors. Terror and reciprocal terror seem doomed to persist.

But there are degrees of extremism, on both sides. Netanyahu offers voters an explicit promise of more violence, and zero concessions to Israel’s foes. Eisenkot cannot credibly promise peace, but he can at least offer less war. A more rational US administration would encourage such an outcome.

If the challenger does become prime minister, however, he will inherit a heavy burden: the obvious failure of Netanyahu’s and Trump’s attempt to batter Iran into submission through air power. A decade ago, a British strategy sage, Michael Howard, told me: “The one thing worse than Iran acquiring nuclear weapons would be a Western attempt to use force to try to stop it doing so.”
Netanyahu would dismiss such counsel as lily-livered. The world should hope that Eisenkot, if he wins, learns something from his predecessor’s bloody mistakes.

items.title: Australia Spring Property Season Sees Auctions Rise but Volumes Stay 34% Lower
body: Australia’s residential real estate activity picked up as the key spring property season finished a second week, although volumes remain subdued amid a housing downturn.

Almost 1,600 home across capital cities were taken to auction this weekend, according to data from property researcher Cotality. While that was an increase from a week ago, volumes were about 34% lower than the same time last year, the data show.

“The spring pattern of more stock coming to market is taking shape, albeit at lower levels than a year ago,” Tim Lawless, research director at Cotality, said in a statement. Activity is set to pick up next week, with more than 1,900 homes scheduled for auction, before easing toward the end of September, he said.
Read more: One of World’s Longest Housing Booms Is Cracking in Sydney

The latest results are a further sign of weakening in the nation’s once-hot housing market following government property tax changes in May and three Reserve Bank interest rate increases. A gauge of house prices slid for five straight months through August, taking the drop from its March peak to 3.6%, according to Cotality.

While the weekend’s auction clearance rates rose to 58.5%, the highest in 19 weeks, they remained well below levels seen a year ago at which time almost three in four homes at auction were sold, Lawless said.

“The lower number of auctions held relative to a year ago reflects fewer new listings coming to market, but also that a larger portion of vendors are opting to sell their home by private treaty rather than auction while clearance rates remain low,” he said.

items.title: Philippines Halts Exports of Fresh Purple Yam as Demand Rises
body: The Philippines has suspended exports of fresh purple yam to protect scarce planting stocks as global demand rises.

The indefinite suspension, imposed in mid-August, covers the crop also known as ube and its propagative planting material, the Department of Agriculture said in a statement on Sunday. The aim is to build production capacity and turn the crop into a bigger export earner, it said.

“We severely lack planting material ourselves, and we don’t want to export it to countries that could use Philippine ube varieties to compete with us,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said.

Philippine ube is increasingly sought by processors and overseas buyers, but planting materials needed to expand production are limited. Ube is processed into powder, jam and paste and used as ingredients in various products from cheesecake to candles.
Exports have been reaching Canada, Middle East and parts of Asia, while US and Europe may be additional markets, the Agriculture department said.

items.title: Brazil's Top Court Gives Police Deadline on Banker's Data
body: Brazilian Chief Justice Edson Fachin has given the Federal Police 24 hours to provide information regarding the custody and condition of the data extracted from the mobile phone of Daniel Vorcaro, former owner of Banco Master, according to a ruling issued Saturday.

This is the latest development in the investigation into the $10 billion Banco Master fraud scandal that threatens to shake up the Brazilian election and has ensnared two Supreme Federal Court judges, Alexandre de Moraes and André Mendonça.

Fachin granted requests from Justices Cristiano Zanin, Moraes and Gilmar Mendes for access to a full copy of the material. Justice Mendonça had previously stated that he has a backup copy — which remains sealed and inaccessible to him — and that the original data is in Federal Police custody.

The Federal Police said in a statement issued Sunday that “it has full technical capacity to produce and forward an identical copy” of the material from Vorcaro’s phone to the offices that requested it.

In a Saturday night decision, Fachin also assumed the role of rapporteur for a proceeding involving Moraes. He ordered that the court presidency receive all files related to two ongoing investigations involving Banco Master and alleged fraud in the country’s social security system.
The chief justice also decided that the full bench will analyze, in separate sessions, the conduct of Justices Mendonça and Moraes regarding investigations linked to the Banco Master case.

On Tuesday, the justices will evaluate alleged messages sent by Vorcaro to a phone number attributed to Moraes. On Sept. 23, the court will hear the case regarding Mendonça’s conduct in overseeing investigations involving court officials.
Fachin’s decision to schedule these matters for different dates runs counter to a request by Moraes for a joint hearing.
On Friday, Mendonça unsealed more documents from probes related to the Master.

Separately, Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino on Sunday unsealed documents of an investigation on the financing of a movie inspired by the life of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The probe focuses on alleged misuse of public funds earmarked by lawmakers including former culture secretary Mario Frias. A spokesperson for Frias didn’t respond to a request for comment.
